title: Talal V. The State,
explainer:
This case involves Talal, who was convicted by a Special Judge (Control of Narcotic Substances) in Gwadar for possessing 8 kilograms of charas (hashish) under section 9(c) of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997. He was sentenced to four years imprisonment and a fine. Talal appealed to the Balochistan High Court, arguing the trial court had misread the evidence and ignored serious contradictions in the prosecution's case.

The High Court agreed with the appellant and acquitted him. It found multiple problems with how the prosecution handled the case: police witnesses gave contradictory accounts, with one saying the recovered charas was weighed collectively and another saying each packet was weighed separately; no identification marks were placed on the recovered material; a lady constable who reportedly accompanied the raiding party and first entered the house was never produced as a witness, with no explanation given; and although samples were supposedly sent for chemical testing the day after recovery, the officer responsible testified he actually took them for testing one and a half months later.

The court held that the prosecution failed to prove an unbroken chain of custody for the narcotics, meaning it could not be certain the substance tested was the same substance actually recovered from the appellant. Citing established principles that even a single reasonable doubt should benefit the accused, the court ruled the prosecution's evidence was unreliable and set aside the conviction, ordering Talal's release. This case highlights how crucial proper evidence handling procedures are in narcotics prosecutions.

title: Abdul Ghaffar V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Abdul Ghaffar, appealing a decision to confiscate a Mercedes Benz container truck that had been used to transport 45.5 kilograms of charas (hashish). The drugs were found hidden in the truck's wheel area when Coast Guards stopped it at a checkpoint. The truck's driver was arrested along with the vehicle and drugs. Ghaffar did not challenge his conviction but only contested the trial court's order confiscating the vehicle, claiming he was its rightful owner based on a sale deed from 2018 and arguing there was no proof he knew the vehicle was being used to smuggle drugs.

The Balochistan High Court rejected his appeal. It found that Ghaffar could not even be legally recognized as the vehicle's owner, since under the Motor Vehicles Ordinance, ownership is defined by vehicle registration, and the truck was never registered in his name. The court also examined Section 32 of the Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, which mandates confiscation of vehicles used to transport narcotics, relying on a Supreme Court precedent (Amjad Khan v. The State) confirming that such vehicles must be forfeited to the state.

This judgment matters because it clarifies that claiming ownership of a vehicle used in drug trafficking requires proper legal registration, not just a private sale agreement, and reinforces that vehicles used to smuggle narcotics are liable to confiscation under the law.

title: Shaheen Alam and 3 others V. Mst. Bibi Salma (Widow) and 7 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Quetta, Balochistan. A widow and her children (the plaintiffs) filed a civil suit claiming that a plot of land belonging to their deceased predecessor had been transferred to relatives (the defendants) through a forged power of attorney. The defendants asked the trial court to reject the plaint, arguing that a similar case about the same property was already pending before the High Court of Sindh in Karachi. The trial court refused to dismiss the plaint but still stayed (paused) the Quetta suit, citing Section 10 of the Civil Procedure Code, which prevents courts from proceeding with a case if the same issue is already being litigated elsewhere between the same parties. The plaintiffs challenged this stay before the District Judge, who set aside the stay order and sent the case back to the trial court to proceed normally. The defendants then approached the Balochistan High Court to restore the stay.

The High Court dismissed their petition. It explained that Section 10 applies only when five specific conditions are met, including that the matter in issue in both suits must be directly and substantially the same. Here, the Karachi case was an administration suit under the Succession Act, concerned with distributing inheritance shares among legal heirs, while the Quetta suit was about cancelling a fraudulent property transfer. Since the causes of action differed, Section 10 did not apply, and the case could proceed in Quetta. This ruling clarifies how courts distinguish between succession/inheritance proceedings and separate property fraud claims.

title: Zahoor Din V. Rehmatullah,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a shop in Hub, Balochistan. Rehmatullah, claiming to be the owner of the shop based on a mutation entry in revenue records, filed an eviction petition against Zahoor Din, who was in possession of the shop, alleging he was a tenant who had stopped paying rent and that the owner also wanted the shop for personal use. Zahoor Din denied being a tenant at all, claiming he had purchased the shop from a previous owner in 2007 and had been occupying it as owner ever since. The Rent Controller sided with Rehmatullah and ordered eviction along with payment of back rent.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court overturned this decision. The Court found that Rehmatullah had failed to prove an essential fact: that a landlord-tenant relationship actually existed between him and Zahoor Din. He produced no independent witnesses and no rent receipts to support this claim. The Court explained that a Rent Controller only has legal authority to order eviction of an actual tenant, not just anyone occupying a property. Even if someone owns property, if the occupant disputes being a tenant, the ownership document alone (like a mutation entry) is not enough to invoke the Rent Controller's jurisdiction. Instead, the owner must go to a regular civil court to establish title and seek possession through proper ownership or trespass proceedings.

title: Niaz Muhammad (Nazak Khan) V. Bibi Khatima and another,
explainer:
This case concerns who is legally responsible for paying child maintenance when the father defaults, and whether a grandfather who was never part of the original lawsuit can be forced to pay.

A mother had won an ex-parte (one-sided) family court order against the father for dissolution of marriage, dower, and child maintenance. When the order went into execution, the father could not be served or located. Without ever making the grandfather a party to the case, the executing family court ordered him to deposit the children's maintenance directly, and later even considered issuing arrest warrants against him when he objected. Both the trial court and the appellate court upheld this, relying on Islamic law principles that a grandfather can be liable for grandchildren's maintenance if the father is poor and unable to earn and the mother too lacks means.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed with how this was applied. It held that under Islamic law (Mulla's Principles, Para 370), a grandfather only becomes liable if it is first proven that the father and mother cannot support the children and that the grandfather himself is financially well-off. Since the grandfather was never made a party to the suit, he had no chance to present evidence on his financial situation. The court also reaffirmed the basic civil law rule that no decree can be enforced against someone who was not party to the case.

The court set aside the orders and sent the matter back so the grandfather could be given a proper hearing before any liability is decided.

title: Muhammad Ali Zahoor, Zonal Director (BISP) V. Government of Pakistan through Secretary Benazir Income Support Programme Islamabad and 3 others,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with a government employee's challenge to his sudden repatriation (sending back) from a deputation post. The petitioner, Muhammad Ali Zahoor, originally worked at Pakistan Broadcasting Corporation in Quetta. In 2021 he successfully applied for a position as Divisional Director at the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) on a three-year deputation basis. However, in October 2022, before completing his three-year term, BISP issued a notification repatriating him back to his parent department without giving specific reasons. He argued this was unlawful, done with ulterior motives, and asked the court to cancel the order so he could complete his full three-year deputation.

The court examined the relevant rules, including BISP's Employees Service Regulations 2018 and the government's ESTA Code, which governs deputation across the civil service. It found that while the normal deputation period is three years (extendable to five), an employee on deputation has no permanent or vested right to stay in the position for the entire term. Citing Supreme Court precedents, the court held that government authorities can repatriate a deputationist at any time, even before the term ends, without needing to give reasons.

This ruling matters because it clarifies that deputation is a temporary arrangement serving organizational needs, not a guaranteed entitlement for the employee, giving departments flexibility to recall officers early.

title: Fazal Muhammad V. Managing Director Sui Gas, Quetta,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute between a gas consumer and Sui Southern Gas Company. The petitioner said an unknown tractor accidentally hit and damaged his house's gas connection during nearby construction work. He reported this to the gas company, but instead of accepting his explanation, the company filed a criminal case against him for gas theft and demanded over 2.5 million rupees as payment for allegedly stolen gas. The petitioner paid a partial installment, allegedly on the company's assurance that the money would be refunded if he was acquitted. He was later acquitted by a sessions court, but when he asked for his money back, the company refused. He then went directly to the Balochistan High Court asking it to cancel the company's claim, restore his gas connection, and order repayment.

The High Court dismissed the petition without deciding the merits of his complaint. It held that disputes between gas consumers and licensed gas companies are specifically governed by the Gas (Theft Control and Recovery) Act, 2016, particularly Section 6, which sets out a detailed procedure for filing complaints and suits before special Gas Utility Courts. Since this law already provides an adequate remedy, the petitioner was required to pursue his claim there first, rather than approaching the High Court directly under its constitutional jurisdiction. The case illustrates the principle that courts will generally not entertain constitutional petitions when an alternate legal remedy exists and has not been used.

title: Syed Taqveem Shah V. Government of Balochistan, Chief Secretary, Quetta and 3 others,
explainer:
This case involved a petition filed before the Balochistan High Court asking the court to stop the provincial government from making transfers and postings of civil servants. The petitioner argued that such transfers, allegedly made by the Chief Minister and Chief Secretary for personal gain ahead of expected general elections, were causing huge losses to the public exchequer and could prejudice the election process. He asked the court to order a complete halt to all civil servant transfers and postings until elections were held and a new government took oath.

The High Court dismissed the petition at the very outset, without going into its merits. The court explained that under Article 199 of the Constitution, only an "aggrieved party" can approach the High Court for such relief. The petitioner had no personal or legal connection to the transfers and postings in question, no property or personal right had been affected, and he could not show any specific harm to himself. Transferring and posting government officials, the court held, is entirely within the discretion of the concerned government departments, and the petitioner had no standing to interfere with that process. The court also noted that at the time, no election date had even been officially announced, weakening the petitioner's claims further.

This case matters because it reaffirms an important constitutional principle: courts cannot be used by ordinary citizens to challenge routine administrative decisions unless they can show they personally suffered some legal injury.

title: Abdul Razaq V. Babal and 5 others,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal against the acquittal of six men accused of murder and armed robbery in Balochistan. The complainant alleged that while traveling by car at night, his group was intercepted by armed men who opened fire, killing his uncle and wounding a young girl, and robbing the passengers of cash and identity cards. The trial court had acquitted the accused, and the complainant challenged that acquittal before the High Court.

The High Court upheld the acquittal, finding serious problems with the prosecution's case. There was an unexplained five-hour delay in filing the police report, even though a police station was only a few kilometers away and the victim had died. The court found the complainant's account implausible, especially his claim that after chasing the armed suspects on foot and finding them at a guesthouse, he still did not alert police or attempt an arrest that night. A key eyewitness, who was allegedly also robbed during the incident, was never presented in court to testify, further weakening the case.

The court reiterated important legal principles: appeals against acquittal are treated differently from appeals against conviction, with courts intervening only when there has been a serious error leading to a miscarriage of justice. It also reaffirmed that a person should not be convicted when reasonable doubt exists. Given the delays, inconsistencies, and missing evidence, the court dismissed the appeal and upheld the acquittal, emphasizing that suspicion or doubt cannot substitute for solid proof in criminal cases.

title: Messrs Welcome Prince Rice Mill through Partners V National Bank of Pakistan through Manager and another,
explainer:
This case involved a rice mill business that had taken a large loan from National Bank of Pakistan, secured against mortgaged property. After the business defaulted on repayment, the Bank sued and won a decree for recovery of over 16 million rupees. During the execution process to enforce this decree, the trial court (acting as the Executing Court) ordered the arrest of the mill owner as a judgment debtor for failing to pay the decretal amount. The mill owner challenged this arrest order before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court examined the legal procedure required before a court can order the arrest of someone who owes money under a decree. Under the Civil Procedure Code, before issuing an arrest warrant against a judgment debtor, the law requires that the person first be given formal notice and an opportunity to explain their financial position. In this case, the record showed no such notice had ever been issued to the petitioner before the arrest warrant was ordered.

The Court ruled that skipping this notice requirement was a serious legal error, since the law is designed to protect people from the humiliation of arrest without first being heard. As a result, the High Court set aside the arrest order and directed the Executing Court to follow proper procedure, meaning it must first issue notice before considering arrest. This judgment reinforces that even when banks are trying to recover unpaid loans, courts must strictly follow due process protections for debtors before resorting to arrest.

title: Ghulam Hussain V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by Ghulam Hussain, who had been convicted of murdering the complainant's brother and causing firearm injuries to another person, along with related charges of attempted murder and rioting with deadly weapons. The Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence and found serious problems with the prosecution's case.

The court identified multiple weaknesses: the complainant's presence at the crime scene was doubtful, since armed attackers supposedly left multiple witnesses unharmed despite an alleged blood feud. An injured witness could not even identify the accused in court, undermining his reliability. No credible motive linking the accused to the crime was established, and evidence suggested the real dispute involved a different tribe than the one to which the accused belonged. Witnesses gave contradictory accounts about timing, events, and how the investigation was conducted, and their statements showed suspicious improvements over time. The witnesses were also found to be "chance witnesses" who lived far from the crime scene, casting doubt on their claimed presence. Additionally, a co-accused had already been acquitted based on the same evidence, and that acquittal was never challenged, weakening the case against the remaining accused further.

Given these serious doubts and inconsistencies, the court ruled that the prosecution's story was not believable and allowed the appeal, overturning the conviction. This case highlights how courts scrutinize witness credibility, motive, and evidentiary consistency before upholding serious criminal convictions.

title: Nisar Ahmed V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case involved an application to cancel a bail order in an assault matter. According to the FIR, a construction dispute at the complainant Nisar Ahmed's house led to a confrontation where several named accused allegedly attacked the complainant's brother with sticks, spades and an axe. Two accused were arrested and faced trial, while three others (respondents) sought and were granted pre-arrest bail by the Additional Sessions Judge. The complainant challenged this bail grant, asking the High Court to cancel it and hand the accused over to police for investigation.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the application and upheld the bail. The judge explained that cancelling bail is different from refusing it in the first place - once bail is granted, courts require strong, exceptional grounds to take it back, not mere allegations. Here, the court found the bail order was not perverse or illegal. It noted a suspicious four-hour-twenty-minute delay in filing the FIR without explanation, suggesting the accused may have been named after deliberation rather than spontaneously. There was also an underlying civil dispute over construction between the parties, and medical evidence showed only one injury, which fell under a bailable provision of the Penal Code rather than the more serious non-bailable sections cited. There was also no proof the accused had misused their bail.

This case illustrates the principle that once bail is granted, higher courts are reluctant to reverse it absent clear illegality or gross error, protecting individual liberty from being curtailed on weak grounds.

The Balochistan High Court granted him bail. The judges found several weaknesses in the prosecution's case that warranted further inquiry. Although police claimed to have received a tip-off and made the arrest in a populated area, they made no effort to include any independent local witness to the arrest and recovery, despite legal requirements for such witnesses when feasible. The court also noted that before the FIR was filed, the accused's mother had already filed a complaint against the same police officer for harassing her family, suggesting the narcotics case might have been fabricated in retaliation. Since the prosecution's case relied entirely on police testimony, the court said this evidence would need careful scrutiny at trial. The accused also had no prior criminal record.

Based on these doubts, the court ruled this was a fit case for bail pending trial, releasing the applicant on surety bonds of Rs. 300,000. The court clarified that its observations were preliminary and would not influence the final outcome of the trial. This case illustrates how procedural lapses by police and potential motives for false implication can be grounds for bail even in serious narcotics cases.

title: Muhammad Hanif V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved Muhammad Hanif, who was convicted under Pakistan's Control of Narcotic Substances Act, 1997, for allegedly possessing 27 kilograms of charas found in the car he was driving in Quetta. Police claimed they acted on a tip-off, stopped his vehicle, and recovered packets of narcotics from under the seats and the trunk.

Hanif appealed his conviction to the Balochistan High Court, and the court overturned it, granting him the benefit of the doubt. The judges found multiple serious flaws in the prosecution's case. The signatures on the evidence parcel produced in court did not match those on other recovery documents, raising doubts about whether the evidence had been properly secured. Witness testimony contradicted the FIR regarding where exactly the drugs were found. The relevant police register documenting how the seized material was stored was never produced. No independent witness from the area was included in the raid, despite it happening in a busy, populated location, and the excuse given—that no one wanted to be involved—was unconvincing. Additionally, the government's chemical analysis of the narcotics didn't follow mandatory procedural rules, undermining the reliability of that report.

The court reaffirmed a key principle of criminal law: even one credible doubt about the prosecution's case is enough to acquit an accused person. Because the prosecution failed to prove safe custody of the evidence and had multiple contradictions, the court ruled it could not be certain the substance tested was actually what was seized from Hanif, and allowed his appeal.

title: Muhammad Bilal and 2 others V. The State,

First, there was an unexplained three-hour delay in filing the police report despite the crime scene being close by, suggesting possible deliberation before the complaint was lodged. Second, the presence of the prosecution's eyewitnesses at the scene was doubtful—inconsistencies existed about the vehicle used to transport the deceased, the witnesses' bloodstained clothes were never produced, and their names were missing from hospital records. Third, the recovery of the murder weapon was suspicious, since investigators had already searched the room without finding it, and later recovery violated proper legal procedure for witnessing searches. Fourth, the chain of custody for the weapon sent to the forensic lab was not properly established, with a 33-day unexplained delay. Finally, medical evidence contradicted witness testimony about timing and the nature of injuries.

title: Shakti Kumar V. Parkash Kumar and another,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute between a landlord and a tenant over a shop used for a confectionery business in Hub, Balochistan. The landlord, Parkash Kumar, filed an application to evict his tenant, Shakti Kumar, arguing that he was the lawful owner of the shop, that there was a written rent agreement between them, that the old building needed major repairs, and that he genuinely needed the shop back for his own personal use. The Rent Controller agreed and ordered the tenant to vacate. The tenant appealed, claiming the landlord did not actually own the shop and had even admitted this during cross-examination, and that the eviction order was based on a misreading of the evidence.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the appeal. It noted that the tenant himself had previously filed a civil suit in which he admitted the landlord was indeed his landlord, and there was a valid rent agreement supported by witness testimony that survived cross-examination. The court reaffirmed a well-established legal principle, previously laid down by the Supreme Court of Pakistan, that in rent disputes only the relationship between landlord and tenant matters, not proof of formal ownership. Since that relationship was clearly established, and the landlord's genuine need for the shop was evident, the tenant's objections had no merit. The eviction order was upheld, and the appeal was dismissed.

title: Dr. Sadrak Jala V. Bishop Fredrick Johan and 4 others,
explainer:
Dr. Sadrak Jala had been Medical Director of Christian Hospital in Quetta, an institution held in trust for the Christian community. A dispute arose over control of the hospital's affairs, and the Bishop and others filed a civil suit seeking a permanent injunction to stop Dr. Jala from interfering in the hospital's management. Along with the suit, they asked the trial court for a temporary injunction under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 of the Civil Procedure Code to maintain the status quo while the case was decided.

The trial court refused to grant this temporary injunction, but on appeal, the Additional District Judge reversed that decision and granted the injunction against Dr. Jala. He then challenged that appellate order before the Balochistan High Court through a civil revision petition.

The High Court explained that a temporary injunction can only be granted if the party asking for it shows three things: a prima facie case, the likelihood of suffering irreparable loss if the injunction is refused, and that the balance of convenience favors them. The court found that the hospital's management and other respondents had not established any of these three requirements. Therefore, the High Court set aside the appellate court's order and restored the trial court's original decision refusing the injunction, allowing Dr. Jala's revision petition.

This case matters because it reaffirms the legal standard courts must apply before granting temporary injunctions, ensuring such powerful interim orders are not issued without proper justification.

title: Dr. Sadrak Jalal and another V. Executive Committee Dioceses of Karachi and Balochistan through Secretary Diocesan Officer Fatima Jinnah Road Karachi and 6 others,
explainer:
This case is about a dispute over who has the legal right to run Christian Hospital, Quetta. Dr. Sadrak Jalal and another petitioner claimed they were properly holding the positions of Medical Director and Administrator of the hospital and asked the court to stop certain church officials (the Diocese and its representatives) from interfering in their duties, pending the appointment of a new Bishop of Karachi and Balochistan Diocese. They filed a civil suit and also sought a temporary injunction to maintain the status quo while the case was heard.

The trial court initially granted the temporary injunction in their favor. However, on appeal, the Additional District Judge overturned this and sided with the respondents, who argued that the petitioners were merely employees (a "master and servant" relationship) and that Dr. Jalal had already retired.

The Balochistan High Court, hearing a revision petition, disagreed with the appellate court. It found no documentary evidence proving an employer-employee relationship between the parties, and noted evidence showing many hospital staff continued working past age 65, indicating there was no fixed retirement age. The High Court held that the petitioners had established a strong prima facie case, would suffer irreparable harm without an injunction, and that the balance of convenience favored them. It therefore restored the trial court's original injunction, allowing the petitioners to continue their roles until the underlying suit is decided. This matters because it protects the status quo in a leadership dispute until the merits are fully litigated.

title: The Director Directorate of Intelligence and Investigation Customs FBR, Quetta through Deputy Director and others V. Messrs International Business Hub and others,
explainer:
This case involved disputes over customs valuation of pistachios imported from Iran into Pakistan. The Directorate of Intelligence and Investigation Customs accused certain importers of under-declaring the value and weight of imported pistachios to evade duties and taxes, claiming losses to government revenue. An adjudicating authority partly agreed, finding the declared value acceptable but flagging the tare weight (packaging weight deducted from total weight) as abnormal. This was appealed to the Customs Appellate Tribunal, which ruled that both the declared value and the tare weight determinations by the Directorate were flawed, since the goods had already been cleared and physically removed, making it impossible to verify claims of excessive tare weight after the fact.

The Balochistan High Court upheld the Tribunal's decision. It held that when two different customs authorities (the Collector and the Directorate) independently determine valuations, any conflict must be resolved by the Director General of Valuation, a step that was never properly taken here. Since the Director General did not object, the Collector's valuation stood as the final and later determination. The Court also found that trying to retroactively adjust tare weight percentages after goods were cleared violated the law, which prohibits amending goods declarations once items leave customs control, especially without clear reasoning for the proposed percentages.

The judgment matters because it reinforces procedural safeguards in customs valuation disputes, preventing arbitrary post-clearance adjustments and clarifying which authority has final say when valuations conflict.

title: Mushtaq Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man named Mushtaq Ahmed who was convicted of murdering an elderly retired government employee, Abdul Ghaffar, and sentenced to life imprisonment by a trial court in Quetta. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The prosecution's case relied mainly on CCTV footage supposedly linking the accused to the crime scene, an alleged confession made to police, recovered cash, and witness testimony. The High Court found serious problems with all of this evidence. The original video footage was never produced in court, no forensic analysis was done to verify it, and no one explained who downloaded it or when, raising the possibility it could have been fabricated or tampered with. The accused's supposed confession to police came three days after his arrest and while he was still in police custody, making it legally inadmissible since confessions to police, especially delayed ones, cannot be used against an accused. The recovery of money from a witness's house was also flawed because it violated procedural rules requiring independent local witnesses, and the property owner himself denied any recovery took place. Additionally, witness statements contradicted each other, and police failed to hold a formal identification parade for a witness who claimed to have seen a suspicious person near the crime scene.

Given these serious gaps and doubts, the High Court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It reaffirmed the principle that even a single reasonable doubt entitles an accused to acquittal as a matter of right, not mercy. The court overturned the conviction and allowed the appeal

title: Naimatullah and others V. The State through Prosecutor General, Balochistan, Quetta and others,
explainer:
Naimatullah was convicted by a trial court in Killa Saifullah for the murder of Muhammad Nabi, having allegedly opened fire on him near a petrol pump. He was sentenced to life imprisonment under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and ordered to pay compensation to the victim's heirs. He appealed the conviction, while the complainant separately filed a revision petition (likely seeking enhancement of sentence).

The Balochistan High Court examined two main defense arguments: first, that there was an unexplained delay in registering the police report (FIR), and second, that the eyewitnesses were unreliable. The court rejected both arguments. On the delay issue, it found the two hour, fifty-minute gap understandable and natural, since the complainant's family first focused on getting medical help for the dying victim before going to police, and the accused was named immediately once the FIR was lodged. On the eyewitness issue, the court held that the two witnesses were not "chance witnesses" merely because they were relatives or from the same community as the victim, since they had a legitimate reason to be near the scene (they ran a business there), their account matched medical evidence, and the incident occurred in daylight among people who already knew each other, ruling out misidentification.

The court dismissed the appeal, upholding the conviction and sentence. The case illustrates how courts assess routine delays in FIR filing and eyewitness credibility, showing that minor procedural or relational issues do not automatically undermine a genuine prosecution case.

title: Muhammad Faisal V. The State through Prosecutor General Balochistan,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted for possessing and transporting narcotics—1800 grams of charas, 200 grams of crystal/ice, and 300 grams of intoxicant tablets—allegedly recovered by police during a patrol after a tip-off. He appealed his conviction to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court overturned the conviction, finding the prosecution's case riddled with serious doubts. Witnesses gave contradictory accounts of basic facts, such as how they learned of the appellant's location, who searched him, and how the seized drugs were weighed and packaged. Notably, the complainant mentioned preparing a parcel that the recovery witness never mentioned, and details about sampling the crystal/ice for testing were missing entirely. The court also found that the case number was written on evidence parcels before the police report was even registered, raising questions about fabrication.

Beyond witness contradictions, the court found the chain of custody broken: there were unexplained delays and discrepancies in when samples were sent to and received by the forensic laboratory, with no record of who held the evidence during a two-day gap. Key documents, like the police patrol log and register entries, were either not properly presented in court or contained no proper record of evidence transfer.

The court ruled that even one serious doubt should benefit the accused, and here there were many. This case reinforces that criminal convictions—especially in narcotics cases carrying severe penalties—require rigorous, consistent evidence and proper documentation, not just police testimony.

title: Dad Muhammad and 4 others V. National Database & Registration Authority through Director General NADRA Quetta,
explainer:
This case concerns five people, the Dad Muhammad group, who sued NADRA (the agency that issues Pakistan's national identity cards) after it refused to give them Computerized National Identity Cards (CNICs) despite their claim of being Pakistani citizens.

The petitioners said their families had owned land in Quetta since 1965-66, long before 1979, and that their uncle had already won a similar case and received his CNIC. They relied on a 2017 government notification that allows people with land records, domicile certificates, or other documents dated before 1978 to have blocked or cancelled CNICs restored. The trial court initially ruled in their favor, but on appeal, the District Judge reversed that decision and dismissed their case. The petitioners then challenged this reversal before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court sided with the petitioners. It found they had produced credible documentary evidence, including old land records, predating 1979, satisfying the requirements of the 2017 notification. The judge emphasized that citizenship is fundamental to a person's constitutional rights, and once someone is recognized as a citizen, they cannot be stripped of that status except through lawful process, stressing the serious human impact of denying citizenship. The Court set aside the appellate court's ruling and restored the trial court's original decision granting the petitioners their CNICs.

This case matters because it reinforces protections against arbitrary denial of citizenship documents and clarifies how historical land and identity records can establish citizenship claims under Pakistani law.

The dispute was resolved through arbitration, and the arbitration award was made a court decree in 1996 by consent of the parties.

Later, the brother's side (the decree holder at the time) filed an execution application in 1998 to enforce the decree, and that application was fully satisfied and closed in 2000. No one challenged this at the time. However, years later, the original plaintiff (Ahmedullah) filed a fresh execution application seeking to enforce the same 1996 decree again. The trial court dismissed this second application, but the appellate court reversed that decision and allowed execution to proceed.

The matter reached the Balochistan High Court, where the petitioners argued that since the decree had already been executed and satisfied once without objection, and that order was never challenged, the second execution attempt was barred by the principle of res judicata (a legal doctrine meaning a matter already finally decided cannot be relitigated).

The High Court agreed. It explained that res judicata exists to bring finality to litigation, prevent harassment through repeated proceedings, and promote judicial economy. Since the first execution had concluded without challenge, the second attempt was barred. The High Court set aside the appellate court's order and dismissed the fresh execution proceedings, restoring finality to the original 2000 decision.

title: Dilawar Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an Afghan national convicted under Pakistan's Foreigners Act for entering the country without legal documents. He was originally charged, and at that hearing explicitly denied the charge and asked for a trial. However, on later hearing dates, after prosecution witnesses failed to appear, he filed an application offering to plead guilty. The trial court accepted this confession and convicted him, sentencing him to time already served plus a small fine.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court examined whether it was lawful for the trial court to accept a guilty plea at this later stage, given that the accused had already denied the charge and asked for trial when it was first framed. The court ruled that once an accused denies the charge and claims trial, the legal provision allowing conviction on a guilty plea becomes inapplicable. Instead, the court must proceed to record full evidence from both prosecution and defense. A confession made much later, after several hearings, could not retroactively substitute for that process.

The court also addressed a separate argument about the appeal being filed late, ruling that the right to appeal is important and delays should generally be excused unless there's no plausible explanation, since technical objections shouldn't block criminal cases from being decided on their merits.

As a result, the conviction was set aside and the case sent back to the trial court to be decided properly after actually recording evidence, rather than relying on a belated guilty plea.

title: Saeed Ahmed and 4 others V. Bibi Khourd and others,
explainer:
This case involved a family dispute over jointly-owned agricultural land in Chaghi, Balochistan. The plaintiffs (petitioners) had filed a lawsuit seeking a declaration that certain properties were jointly owned by the family and should be divided among them. During the proceedings, they filed an application asking the court to amend their original lawsuit under a procedural rule (Order VI, Rule 17 of the Civil Procedure Code), claiming they had discovered that one of the defendants had secretly transferred property into his own name without the knowledge of the plaintiffs' mother.

Both the trial court and the appeals court (Additional District Judge) rejected this amendment request, so the plaintiffs approached the High Court.

The High Court upheld the lower courts' decisions and dismissed the petition. It ruled that when someone asks to amend a legal pleading, they must clearly and specifically state exactly what changes they want made and exactly where in the document those changes should go. Vague or general requests for amendment are not acceptable. The court found that the plaintiffs' application failed to specify what exactly they wanted added or changed. Additionally, the court noted this was actually a second amendment request, and the plaintiffs were essentially repeating facts they had already been allowed to include earlier, suggesting they were delaying the case rather than genuinely needing changes.

This ruling matters because it reinforces an important procedural principle: courts require precision and clarity in legal filings, and parties cannot use vague amendment requests to stall litigation indefinitely.

title: Aamir Ali V. The State,
explainer:
Two men were accused of firing on a house in a land dispute, killing a five-year-old boy with a stray bullet. Both were tried together under the same murder charge, but the trial court convicted only Aamir Ali, sentencing him to death, while acquitting his co-accused Ali Raza, whose alleged role was identical.

The Balochistan High Court's Sibi Bench heard Aamir Ali's appeal along with the mandatory murder reference. It found that the evidence against Aamir Ali was essentially the same as that used against the acquitted co-accused. Applying the rule of consistency, the court held that once eyewitnesses were disbelieved regarding one accused, their testimony could not be relied upon against another accused unless independently corroborated - and no such independent proof existed here.

The court also noted serious flaws in the site plan: it did not record whose information it was based on, and the eyewitnesses gave no indication either, making the site map unreliable in a murder case. Reaffirming established principles that convictions require direct, substantive evidence and that even a single reasonable doubt must benefit the accused, the court set aside the conviction.

As a result, Aamir Ali's appeal was allowed, his death sentence was overturned, and he was acquitted. This case highlights how courts guard against inconsistent treatment of co-accused facing identical evidence, and stresses the importance of properly documented investigative procedures in criminal trials.

title: Abdul Wali and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about three men convicted of murdering a man during an attempted robbery in Quetta. The trial court had found appellant Barat guilty of murder under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code, sentencing him to life imprisonment, while convicting co-accused Noorullah and Abdul Wali under Section 302(c) with Section 34 (common intention) for lesser terms, plus robbery-related charges for all three.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found serious flaws in how the trial court wrote its judgment. First, the trial court contradicted itself: in one part it said the accused acted with common intention to kill, but later said the fatal shot was fired out of panic, implying no prior intent. Second, although all three men were originally charged together under the "common intention" provision (Section 34), the trial court ended up judging each man's guilt separately, without clearly deciding whether they had acted jointly with shared intent, as the law requires when people are charged as a group.

The High Court ruled that this confused, contradictory, and legally incomplete judgment violated Section 367 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which requires judgments to clearly explain the reasoning behind a conviction. Because the flaws were too serious to overlook, the court could not uphold the convictions as written. Instead of acquitting or deciding the case itself, it sent the case back to the trial court, ordering it to rewrite the judgment properly within two months based on the existing evidence, ensuring clear findings on each accused's role and intent.

title: Kamal Ashraf and others V. Atique-Ur-Rehman and others,
explainer:
This case is about whether a lawyer can file important legal documents on behalf of clients without the clients actually signing them or knowing the contents.

The petitioners had filed a civil suit for declaration and permanent injunction. During the case, their previous lawyer filed a "replication" (a formal reply to the other side's written statement) but only the lawyer signed it, not the clients themselves. The petitioners later discovered this document was being used in another related case, and claimed they never knew about it or authorized its specific content. They challenged the replication in the trial court and then in a civil revision, but both courts rejected their objections, so they approached the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court ruled in favor of the petitioners. It held that under the Civil Procedure Code, certain pleadings—including replications—must be signed by the party themselves or a properly authorized agent, not just the lawyer. The court emphasized that lawyers cannot make factual claims or seek substantial relief based on facts that are within the personal knowledge of their clients, since only the client can vouch for those facts. Since the replication wasn't signed by the petitioners, the court found it doubtful that it was filed on their actual instructions. The court set aside the lower courts' orders and ruled the replication invalid.

This case matters because it reinforces the limits of a lawyer's authority—lawyers cannot unilaterally commit clients to factual assertions in court without proper authorization and signatures, protecting clients from being bound by statements they never approved.

title: Mst. Samina Bibi V. Abdul Khaliq and another,
explainer:
This case is about a wife who sought cancellation of pre-arrest bail granted to a man accused of murdering her husband. Samina Bibi's husband, Samiullah, was shot dead, and she filed a police report naming Abdul Khaliq (respondent No.1) and four others as suspects, alleging the killing was connected to threats over her husband's marriage to a woman named Maira, whose family had reportedly objected. Abdul Khaliq sought and was granted pre-arrest bail by a trial court, partly because he claimed he was elsewhere at the time of the murder, attending an official meeting at the Chief Secretary's office, supported by CCTV footage, a certificate, and an attendance sheet listing his name. The widow challenged this bail grant before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court dismissed her petition. It found that Abdul Khaliq was not actually named in an earlier complaint about threats against the deceased, weakening the case against him. More importantly, the court explained that granting bail and cancelling bail are governed by different legal standards: courts are generally reluctant to cancel bail once granted unless there's evidence the accused misused that bail (such as tampering with evidence or fleeing). Since the petitioner couldn't show any such misuse or violation of bail conditions, the court held the trial court's decision wasn't unreasonable or arbitrary, and upheld the bail.

This case illustrates the important legal distinction between initially opposing bail and later seeking its cancellation, showing that stronger evidence is needed for the latter

title: Ghulam Muhammad V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns Ghulam Muhammad, an accused in a murder case, who had absconded from justice for years. Because he could not be arrested, the court had earlier proclaimed him an offender and ordered attachment of his immovable property under Section 88 of the Criminal Procedure Code, so as to pressure him into appearing before the court. Years later, in December 2023, he was arrested and put on trial. He then applied under Section 89 Cr.P.C. to get his attached property released, arguing he never knew about the attachment earlier. The trial court dismissed his application, saying it was filed too late, beyond the two-year limitation period from the date of attachment.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed. It held that the two-year limitation period only starts running from the date the property is actually and physically attached on the ground, with proper legal steps such as involvement of the District Collector and taking possession. Here, none of that had happened, the accused had remained in continuous possession of his land throughout, and he only learned of the attachment after his arrest. Therefore, limitation should be counted from his date of knowledge, not from 2016. Since the purpose of attachment, securing his appearance in court, had already been achieved through his arrest, and the attachment order had never been properly implemented, the court ruled that the property must be released. This judgment clarifies how limitation periods and procedural requirements under Sections 88 and 89 Cr.P.C. must be strictly followed before an absconder's property can be permanently forfeited.

title: Roshan Bibi V. Assistant Director (In-Charge) Manager National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA), Loralai and 2 others,
explainer:
This case was about a woman, Roshan Bibi, who wanted her correct date of birth reflected in her official records. She sued NADRA and the education board to correct this and issue revised documents.

Both the trial court and the first appellate court dismissed her case, apparently ruling against her partly on the ground that her claim was filed too late (barred by limitation), and questioning whether she had proven her correct birth date.

The Balochistan High Court, hearing her revision petition, disagreed with the lower courts. It found that the school register entry was made when she was just ten years old, so she could not have manipulated it herself, and that the authorities had not actually disputed the authenticity of her school documents. The High Court concluded she had successfully proven her correct date of birth through her school records.

As a result, the High Court set aside the decisions of both lower courts, allowed her revision petition, and ordered NADRA and the education authorities to correct her date of birth in line with her school record. This case matters because it shows courts can intervene to protect a person's right to accurate identity documents when credible, undisputed childhood records support their claim, even after lower courts had rejected it.

title: Mst. Safia and another V. Sabit Ali and another,
explainer:
This case involved a family court dispute over dowry articles worth 100 misqal of gold. After a woman named Mehreen died, her parents filed a suit against her husband seeking recovery of the dowry articles she had brought into her marriage. The husband objected, arguing that Mehreen's parents had no legal standing to bring this claim in a Family Court, especially since a son had been born from the marriage. The trial court agreed and dismissed the suit, and the appellate court upheld that decision. The parents then approached the Balochistan High Court through a constitutional petition, asking that the matter be sent back for a full trial.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It explained that Family Courts have a limited jurisdiction, restricted only to matters specifically listed in the Family Courts Act, such as dower, maintenance, custody, and dowry disputes between spouses. Claims relating to inheritance or a deceased person's estate (Tarka), including distribution among heirs, fall outside this jurisdiction. Since the parents were essentially asking for their share of the deceased daughter's estate rather than resolving a dispute between spouses, their case did not qualify as a matter a Family Court could hear.

This ruling clarifies that Family Courts are meant for disputes arising directly from marriage between spouses, not for inheritance claims by relatives after a spouse's death, which must instead be pursued through proper civil or succession proceedings.

title: Sona Khan and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case concerns two men, Sona Khan and Bashir Ahmed, who were convicted by a trial court in Dukki, Balochistan, and sentenced to life imprisonment for the kidnapping and murder of the complainant's son. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The prosecution's case rested on circumstantial evidence: an alleged extra-judicial confession, a judicial confession recorded before a magistrate, "last seen" testimony from two witnesses, and recoveries of items like a spade, SIM card, and cell phone based on the accused's disclosures. A skeleton, found in a jungle less than a month after the victim went missing, was identified as the deceased through clothes and hair, but doctors could not determine the cause of death since only bones remained.

The High Court found serious problems with every piece of evidence. The extra-judicial confession was unreliable since the cause of death was never established. The judicial confession was recorded improperly, violating legal safeguards, making it inadmissible. The two "last seen" witnesses were close relatives of the complainant who delayed reporting what they saw for 24 days, making their testimony suspicious. The physical recoveries were made in a staggered, day-by-day manner without proper independent witnesses, violating procedural law. The court also noted no evidence explained how a body could fully skeletonize in under a month.

Since circumstantial evidence must form an unbroken chain linking the accused to the crime, and here multiple links were missing, the court gave the accused benefit of the doubt and acquitted them, all

title: Changaiz Khan and others V. The State and others,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court, deciding an appeal by Changaiz Khan and others who had been convicted of murdering two sons of a complainant and injuring two others in a gun attack, along with related charges of rioting and unlawful assembly.

The High Court overturned the convictions, finding the prosecution's case riddled with serious weaknesses. First, the complainant's own conduct was suspicious: rather than rushing his injured and dying sons to hospital or immediately alerting police, he stayed home while neighbors handled the emergency, contrary to how a father would naturally react. Second, there was an unexplained delay of one hour and forty minutes in filing the police report, even though the police station was only three kilometers away. Third, statements of key eyewitnesses were recorded 8 to 10 days late, with no credible explanation, even though the investigating officer had met these witnesses earlier at the hospital. One crucial injured witness's statement was never even recorded. The court also found that the claim that all accused shared a common criminal intent under Section 149 was not proven, since specific roles weren't clearly assigned to each accused. Additionally, important documents like the written complaint, the formal statement (fard-e-bayan), and recovery memos for evidence were never produced in court.

Because of these cumulative failures, the court ruled the prosecution had not proven guilt beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted the appellants, highlighting how procedural lapses and withheld evidence can undermine even serious criminal cases.

title: Muhammad Ajmal V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a road accident in Gwadar where a gas tanker driven by Muhammad Ajmal allegedly hit a car, killing two women and injuring three others. Police registered a case against the driver and seized the tanker as part of the investigation. Ajmal, after being released on bail, applied to the trial court asking for the vehicle to be released to him under Section 516-A of the Criminal Procedure Code, which deals with custody of property during trial. The Sessions Judge in Gwadar rejected this request, so Ajmal challenged that decision before the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court ruled in his favor. It explained that under the law, property can only be withheld by a court if it is either the actual subject of the crime or was used to commit the offense. The judge found that a vehicle involved in a rash or negligent driving accident is not considered a weapon used to commit the crime in the legal sense. The court also noted the tanker belonged to a company, not the accused personally, and the company had no role in the offense. Since Ajmal was the last person in possession of the vehicle and no one else claimed it, the court held it should be returned to him for safekeeping while the case proceeds. The petition was allowed, and the vehicle was ordered released to him.

This case matters because it clarifies when police can hold onto vehicles involved in accidents and reaffirms that ownership and lack of criminal culpability should guide custody decisions during criminal trials.

title: Shaukat Ali V. The State,
explainer:
This is a criminal appeal decided by the Balochistan High Court involving a man named Shaukat Ali, who had been convicted by a trial court for possessing 230 grams of charas (a narcotic substance) and sentenced to ten months imprisonment plus a fine.

The High Court overturned the conviction after finding serious flaws in the prosecution's case. First, there was a major contradiction between witnesses: the complainant claimed he personally weighed the recovered drugs and prepared sample parcels, while the investigating officer claimed he did that job himself. This inconsistency undermined the reliability of the evidence. Second, the prosecution failed to prove the samples were safely transported to the laboratory for testing—the police constable who allegedly carried the samples was never questioned or brought to testify, leaving a gap in the chain of custody. Third, the chemical examiner's report, which would have confirmed the substance was actually a narcotic, was never properly presented and admitted as evidence during the trial, despite being part of the case file.

Given these lapses, the court held that any single reasonable doubt is enough to entitle an accused person to acquittal—not as leniency, but as a legal right. Since the prosecution's evidence was unreliable and incomplete on multiple points, the court set aside the conviction and allowed the appeal, meaning Shaukat Ali was cleared of the charges. The case highlights how procedural rigor in handling evidence and witness testimony is essential to secure a valid conviction in narcotics cases.

title: M/s. Mehtarzai & Brothers Construction Company through Muhammad Ibrahim V. Government of Balochistan through its Secretary Home Department and others,
explainer:
This case involved a construction company, Mehtarzai & Brothers, that had bid for maintenance and facilities work tendered by the Provincial Disaster Management Authority (PDMA) in Balochistan. The company's bid was rejected and the contract was instead awarded to another party. Mehtarzai filed a complaint with PDMA's Grievance Redressal Committee, arguing that the rejection violated public procurement rules and that it had actually met all requirements. The Committee rejected the complaint without giving the company a hearing. Instead of appealing that decision further, the company went straight to the Balochistan High Court asking it to declare the award illegal and order the contract be given on merit.

The High Court dismissed the petition without examining the merits of the dispute. It held that the Balochistan Public Procurement Regulatory Authority Rules, 2014 provide a complete grievance mechanism, including a right to appeal an adverse Grievance Redressal Committee decision to a Review Committee or Board. Since the company had not used this appeal route before rushing to court, its petition was premature. The Court reiterated the settled constitutional principle that courts will not exercise their extraordinary writ jurisdiction under Article 199 when an adequate alternative remedy exists.

This ruling matters because it reinforces that companies and bidders disputing government procurement decisions must first exhaust all remedies provided under procurement rules before seeking court intervention, preserving the specialized administrative process for resolving such disputes.

The High Court dismissed the department's appeal, upholding the lower rulings. Since the department failed to provide solid evidence or conduct proper investigation before issuing its notice, its case could not stand.

title: Read Hamood ur Rehman Commission Report
explainer:
This is an excerpt from the Hamoodur Rahman Commission's Supplementary Report, an official inquiry set up by the Pakistani government to investigate the 1971 war that led to the surrender of Pakistani forces in East Pakistan (now Bangladesh) and the creation of Bangladesh. The Commission, headed by Chief Justice Hamoodur Rahman along with two other senior judges, examined hundreds of witnesses including top military officers involved in the conflict, such as Lt. Gen. Niazi, who signed the surrender to Indian forces.

This particular chapter focuses on the moral conduct of senior army officers stationed in East Pakistan. The Commission found that repeated military involvement in governing the country, starting with martial law in 1958 and worsening after 1969, corrupted army leadership. Officers were found to have illegally acquired property, engaged in improper business dealings, and lived immoral lifestyles that undermined their military effectiveness. The report details specific allegations against named officers, including Gen. Niazi's reputation for sexual misconduct and alleged abuse of position for personal profit, as well as accusations of looting, currency misappropriation, and theft by several other commanders and their units.

This document matters because it represents part of Pakistan's own official reckoning with the causes of its military defeat and the loss of East Pakistan, highlighting how corruption and moral decay within army leadership contributed to the crisis, and calling for further investigation or trial of implicated officers.

title: Saima V. Government Of Balochistan,
explainer:
This case involved a woman named Saima who challenged the appointment of someone else to the post of Laboratory Assistant at a government girls' high school in Quetta. The job had been advertised with a specific requirement: applicants needed a Secondary School Certificate (Matric) in Science. Saima, however, held a Matric certificate in Arts, not Science. Her argument was that since she was the only candidate from the local union council, she deserved the job anyway, and she also pointed out that her uncle had donated the land on which the school was built.

The Balochistan High Court rejected her petition. It explained that a person can only invoke the court's constitutional jurisdiction (Article 199) if a genuine legal or fundamental right has been violated. Since Saima did not meet the minimum qualification for the post, she had no legal right to the job in the first place, and therefore could not be considered an "aggrieved person" entitled to challenge the appointment in court. The court emphasized that governments are entitled to set qualification standards for posts, especially given scientific and technical advancement, and that unqualified candidates cannot be appointed merely because no other local applicant exists, or based on unrelated considerations like land donations.

The petition was dismissed outright, reinforcing the principle that merit and prescribed qualifications must be respected in public sector appointments, and that courts will not entertain claims from applicants who don't meet basic eligibility criteria.

title: Mitha Khan Umrani V. Federation Of Pakistan,
explainer:
This case concerns a man who applied for a government job as a "Micro Form Technician" advertised through the National Assembly Secretariat. The advertisement required candidates to have completed Intermediate in Science along with experience in microfilming, and set a maximum age limit of 25 years. The petitioner, however, had completed Intermediate in Arts, was 35 years old, and lacked the required experience at the relevant cut-off date. He complained that he was neither called for an interview nor informed about the outcome of a written test he had taken, and argued he deserved consideration, citing age relaxations available to government servants and a training certificate in microfilming obtained later.

The government responded that the post itself had been abolished and redesigned as a "Data Entry Operator" position due to becoming technologically obsolete, and that the petitioner had not participated in the new recruitment process.

The Balochistan High Court dismissed the petition, holding that the petitioner clearly did not meet the minimum qualifications or age limit for the advertised post, even after accounting for permissible age relaxations. The court emphasized that the government has the authority to set qualifications for posts, considering scientific and technical advancements, and that unqualified candidates cannot be appointed in violation of prescribed criteria. It also held that abolishing a post is within the government's discretionary power. This case reinforces that eligibility must strictly match advertised qualifications and that courts will not interfere with legitimate administrative decisions about job requirements.

title: Ubaidullah and another V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court involved two petitioners, Ubaidullah and Ain-ud-Din, who asked the court to quash a criminal case registered against them. The complainant, a coal mine owner, alleged that in connection with an outstanding business debt for coal mining commission, the petitioners issued him a cheque worth over 1.2 million rupees, which was later dishonoured when presented to the bank. Police registered a case involving cheating, forgery, and dishonestly issuing a cheque.

The petitioners argued the matter was purely a civil contractual dispute and that they had already repaid a large portion of the outstanding amount, so criminal proceedings should be dropped. The court disagreed. It held that issuing a bounced cheque, even arising from a civil obligation, can still separately constitute a criminal offence under section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code. Civil and criminal proceedings can run side by side, and one does not cancel out the other.

The court also noted that police had already completed their investigation and formally submitted the case (challan) to the trial court, so it would be inappropriate for the High Court to intervene at this stage. The petitioners still had the option to seek relief directly from the trial court. For these reasons, the petition to quash the case was dismissed, meaning the criminal case against them will proceed.

title: Mst. Zohra and others V. Tariq Murtaza,
explainer:
The case involved a landlord-tenant dispute under the West Pakistan Urban Rent Restriction Ordinance, 1959. The appellants (Mst. Zohra and others) claimed to be landlords of a house in Quetta, alleging that the tenants had defaulted on rent, sublet the property without permission, and that the landlords needed the house for their own genuine use. They sought eviction of the respondents. The tenants denied any landlord-tenant relationship existed with the appellants and argued the eviction application was not maintainable.

The Rent Controller dismissed the eviction petition, finding serious problems with the landlords' case. Notably, the appellants claimed the house was rented to the tenants' predecessor in 1995, but evidence showed that person had actually died in 1990, before the alleged tenancy even began. There was also no proof that any rent had ever been paid directly to the appellants, and evidence suggested another person held a civil court decree establishing ownership of the house. The court found the tenants' version of events more credible than the landlords'.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court upheld the Rent Controller's decision, ruling that disputes over property ownership and title fall within the jurisdiction of civil courts, not rent controllers, who only have authority when a genuine landlord-tenant relationship is established. Since the appellants failed to prove such a relationship, and the underlying ownership dispute remained unresolved, the eviction appeal was dismissed. The case highlights that rent controllers cannot decide ownership disputes and eviction claims

title: Abdul Hadi V. Government of Balochistan, Local Government Rural Development Agrovilles Department,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over how local council wards were drawn up in District Pishin, Balochistan. After the Balochistan Local Government Act, 2010 was passed, authorities invited the public to submit proposals and objections regarding ward boundaries. The petitioner, Abdul Hadi, took part in this process along with other residents, submitting suggestions over more than a year. However, when the government issued its final delimitation notification in October 2013, the petitioner felt his proposals had been ignored. He approached the High Court asking it to strike down the notification and order the authorities to redraw the wards according to his recommendations.

The court dismissed the petition. It found that the government had properly followed the procedures laid out in the 2010 Act and the accompanying Delimitation Rules of 2011, and that the petitioner had actually participated throughout the process. Crucially, the Rules provided a specific right of appeal against delimitation decisions, which had to be filed within seven days. The petitioner never used this appeal option. The court also noted that the Electoral Rolls Act, 1974 does not allow changes to ward boundaries once the election schedule has been announced.

The judgment reinforces a basic principle of Pakistani law: a constitutional petition to the High Court can only be filed when no other legal remedy is available. Since the petitioner had a proper appeal route he failed to use, his direct petition to the court was not allowed, and it was dismissed.

title: Muhammad Khan V. Amanullah,
explainer:
Muhammad Khan was Chairman of the District Zakat and Ushr Committee in Sibi. Wanting to contest the upcoming local council elections, he resigned from this position on 30 October 2013, shortly before submitting his nomination papers for a seat on the Municipal Committee, Sibi. A returning officer initially accepted his nomination papers, but a rival candidate appealed, and the District and Sessions Judge, acting as Appellate Authority, rejected the papers on the ground that six months had not passed since Khan's resignation, as required by law.

Khan challenged this rejection before the Balochistan High Court, arguing the Zakat Committee post was unpaid and part-time and that he had resigned merely to avoid political criticism, so no disqualification should apply.

The High Court disagreed. It held that anyone administering Zakat funds is legally considered a "public servant," and such officials are barred from taking part in political activity. Since local council elections count as political activity, and the law requires a six-month gap after leaving such public service before running for office, Khan remained disqualified. The court reasoned this waiting period exists precisely to prevent any lingering influence from the office affecting election results. Since Khan himself resigned specifically because he knew he could not otherwise contest while holding that post, the court found the Appellate Authority's decision lawful and dismissed his petition, upholding the rejection of his nomination papers.

title: Haider Ali Khan Jamali V. Returning Officer/Adc Jaffarabad,
explainer:
This case involved a candidate, Haider Ali Khan Jamali, who wanted to contest a local government election from Ward No. 2 of Municipal Committee Usta Muhammad in Balochistan. He had originally submitted nomination papers from multiple constituencies, including one where his name actually appeared on the electoral roll, but withdrew from those and sought to contest from a ward where his name was not registered as a voter. His nomination was initially accepted by the Returning Officer, but on appeal by another candidate, the Appellate Authority rejected his papers because his name was not on the electoral roll for that ward. He then approached the High Court seeking a direction that he be included in the list of validly nominated candidates.

The High Court dismissed the petition. It held that under the Balochistan Local Government Act, 2010, a candidate must be a registered voter in the electoral roll of the relevant ward to qualify for election there. It also relied on Section 20 of the Electoral Rolls Act, 1974, which bars any correction or revision of electoral rolls once an election schedule has been announced. Since the petitioner had over five months before the election schedule was announced to correct his voter registration but failed to do so, the court found the electoral roll could not be corrected at this late stage.

This case matters because it clarifies that candidates must ensure their voter registration is accurate well before elections are announced, and courts cannot override statutory deadlines for correcting electoral rolls once the election process has begun.

title: Ejaz Ahmed V. The State,
explainer:
Ejaz Ahmed was accused, along with an absconding co-accused, of shooting and killing Muhammad Anwar in Quetta in October 2011. He was already in custody and had also been charged in the murder case, and applied for post-arrest bail after a sessions judge had earlier rejected his request.

His lawyer argued that two other co-accused, alleged only of instigating the crime, had already been acquitted in the same trial, so the applicant deserved similar treatment. He also argued the eyewitnesses were the deceased's relatives and thus biased, that there was an unexplained delay in reporting the crime to police, and that the case needed further investigation.

The Balochistan High Court rejected the bail application. It held that the acquittal of the co-accused did not help the applicant, because they were only accused of encouraging the crime while he was accused of actually carrying it out, so the cases were not comparable. The court also said the legal principle that lying about one part of a case discredits the whole case does not apply in criminal justice, and courts must separate reliable evidence from unreliable evidence. Being related to the victim did not automatically make witnesses unreliable. The court also found that the applicant had been a fugitive for over two years, which, combined with other evidence, suggested guilt, and that the reporting delay of just over an hour was not significant. Bail was therefore refused.

title: Abdul Lateef and 13 Others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved fourteen people from Zhob, Balochistan, who were accused of beating relatives during a family dispute in November 2011. The complainant said he and three others were attacked with spades and sticks while trying to help his cousin, who was being beaten. All fourteen accused were convicted by a magistrate for causing injuries, and this conviction was upheld on appeal by the Sessions Judge. They then challenged their convictions before the Balochistan High Court.

The defense argued that the case stemmed from a land dispute among relatives, that elderly family members had been wrongly implicated, that witnesses gave contradictory statements about motive, and that the charge sheet did not clearly specify what role each accused person played.

The High Court found that while the motive (land dispute) was proven and the injuries were confirmed by medical evidence, only five of the fourteen accused had been given specific roles in the incident by witnesses. The other eight were vaguely implicated simply because they belonged to the same family, apparently to humiliate the opposing side. The court held that injured witnesses do not always tell the complete truth, and doubtful cases must benefit the accused as a matter of right, not mercy.

The court acquitted eight of the fourteen accused for lack of clear evidence, while upholding convictions for five people who were specifically identified as participants, with punishments including fines instead of harsher terms given their clean records. This case highlights the importance of assigning individual responsibility rather than convicting entire family groups collectively.

title: Collector of Customs, through Additional Collector of Customs V. Messrs Haji Ballow Khan and another,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the internal procedures of the Customs, Excise and Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal. The Customs Department challenged an order passed by the Tribunal's Chairman, arguing that he had decided the case sitting alone as a single member without properly constituting a two-member bench, as generally required under Section 194C of the Customs Act, 1969.

The Balochistan High Court examined the law governing how the Tribunal organizes its benches. It held that while the Chairman has administrative discretion to distribute cases among Tribunal members, this discretion is not unlimited. Before assigning a case to a single member, the Chairman must record reasons and can only do so for matters already allotted to a two-member bench, using a member who was part of that bench. The Chairman cannot simply retain and decide a case himself without following this process, except in genuine situations of urgency, and even then he must record his reasons.

Since the Chairman had decided the matter without properly constituting a bench or justifying single-member adjudication, the Court ruled his order was "coram non judice" (issued without proper jurisdiction) and therefore invalid. The Court set aside the order and directed the Tribunal to reconstitute a proper bench and rehear the case from scratch.

This judgment matters because it clarifies the limits of a tribunal chairman's administrative power and reinforces that procedural safeguards ensuring fair, properly constituted adjudication cannot be bypassed even for convenience or urgency.
