title: Abu Bakar Siddique and another V. State and another,
explainer:
This is a Balochistan High Court judgment involving a man convicted of murdering his wife, Tayaba Ibrahim. Police found him standing beside her body at a hospital, and he reportedly told an officer that he had assaulted her during a quarrel, leading to her death. He was convicted by the trial court under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced to life imprisonment, plus a separate five-year sentence for causing hurt. He appealed his conviction, while the victim's mother filed a separate petition seeking a harsher sentence, namely the death penalty.

The High Court examined the evidence, which was largely circumstantial, including an extra-judicial confession made to police (not directly admissible as formal confession evidence, though relevant as part of the immediate aftermath of the crime under the "res gestae" principle) and the fact that the husband was the last person seen with his wife before her death. The court held that when someone is last seen with a victim, they must reasonably explain the circumstances of death; failure to do so strengthens the case against them.

However, the court found evidence suggesting the killing occurred during a sudden quarrel possibly triggered by provocation, rather than being premeditated. Because of this mitigating circumstance, the court ruled that the death penalty was not warranted, and upheld the life sentence instead. The appeal was dismissed, and the request to enhance the sentence was rejected. The case illustrates how courts weigh circumstantial evidence and provocation in murder sentencing.

title: Abu Bakar Siddique V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man convicted of murdering his wife. The prosecution's case rested on circumstantial evidence, since there were no eyewitnesses to the actual killing. When police arrived at the hospital after being told an injured woman had died, they found the husband present, and he told the officer that he had assaulted his wife during a quarrel, causing the injuries that led to her death. This account became the basis of the FIR.

At trial, the husband changed his story, claiming unknown intruders had attacked his house and injured his wife while he tried to fight them off. The court rejected this defence, finding it fabricated and unsupported by evidence—for instance, the household guards knew nothing of any break-in, nothing was stolen, and the extent and nature of the injuries (including cigarette burns) were inconsistent with a robbery gone wrong.

The court held that his own admission to the officer, made before he had reason to fabricate a story, along with his failure to plausibly explain his wife's unnatural death while she was last seen with him, strongly corroborated his guilt. His conviction was upheld.

However, the court reduced his death sentence to life imprisonment, reasoning that the killing may have occurred in a moment of sudden provocation during a domestic quarrel rather than as a premeditated act, which the court treated as a mitigating factor. The judgment clarifies when circumstantial evidence can support serious criminal convictions and how provocation can affect sentencing.

title: Bhooral Khan V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved a man, Bhooral Khan, who was accused of murdering Raham Dil by firing on him with a Kalashnikov during a dispute connected to an alleged ox theft. After the FIR was lodged, the accused could not be found, so the trial court declared him a proclaimed offender and proceeded to try and convict him in his absence, ultimately sentencing him to death. Years later, when he was arrested, he asked the court to reconsider his case under a provision of the Anti-Terrorism Act that allows a person convicted in absentia to seek a fresh hearing, arguing he never knew about the case against him and had not deliberately evaded justice. The trial court rejected this request.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court found that the law required the trial court to properly investigate whether the accused's absence was truly willful before proceeding with a trial in absentia. Since this mandatory inquiry was not carried out, and the trial appeared to have moved forward hastily without proper appreciation of evidence, the accused was denied his constitutional right to a fair trial, guaranteed under Article 10-A of the Constitution.

The High Court set aside the death sentence and conviction and sent the case back to the trial court to be heard afresh, properly this time. The judgment reinforces that even proclaimed offenders are entitled to fair trial protections, and courts cannot bypass Supreme Court precedents or constitutional safeguards when convicting someone who was tried without being present.

title: Aziz Ullah V. The State,
explainer:
Aziz Ullah was convicted by a trial court in Quetta under Section 377 of the Pakistan Penal Code for allegedly committing sodomy on a six-year-old boy, and sentenced to five years rigorous imprisonment plus a fine. He appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court closely examined the evidence. The child victim testified at trial but never actually described any unnatural sexual act happening to him, only that the accused removed his clothing and used abusive language. The medical officer's report found "tenderness" in the victim's anal region and concluded this indicated sexual assault, but the court noted that Section 377 requires proof of penetration to establish the offence, and the victim never mentioned penetration. The court also found the medical examination flawed: no proctoscopy instrument was used to properly collect samples, no injuries or abrasions were found, and tenderness alone could easily result from unrelated causes like constipation. Additionally, there was no positive forensic report confirming semen stains matched between the victim's and accused's clothing, and the police never even obtained the accused's blood group for comparison.

Given these serious gaps, the court held that the medical evidence did not corroborate the witness testimony, and the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction and sentence were set aside, and Aziz Ullah was acquitted.

This case highlights how convictions in serious sexual offence cases require solid, corroborated evidence, not just inconclusive medical findings.

title: Muhammad Azam Davi V. The State through FIA,
explainer:
This case involved a bail application by Muhammad Azam Davi, a former Secretary of the Balochistan Provincial Assembly, who was accused under Pakistan's Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016. The complaint alleged that sensitive internal information from the Assembly, including car repair estimates and security-related meeting minutes, was leaked and posted on social media accounts. A co-accused, who ran the social media pages, told investigators that the applicant had supplied him with this information, allegedly out of personal grudge after the Speaker of the Assembly terminated his job extension.

The applicant argued there was no direct evidence against him, that the offences he was charged with did not actually apply to the facts, and that the case was really about personal enmity rather than a genuine cybercrime. The Speaker's counsel and investigating agency opposed bail, arguing the leak endangered the Assembly's security and dignity.

The Balochistan High Court found several unresolved questions: whether the FIR actually supported charges like identity misuse or stalking, whether the leak was a personal vendetta or something more serious like terrorism, and importantly, whether a co-accused's statement implicating the applicant could even be used as evidence against him under the Qanun-e-Shahadat (Evidence) Order. Since these issues required deeper investigation and the applicant wasn't needed for further inquiry, the court granted him bail. This shows how courts scrutinize whether cybercrime charges are properly supported by evidence before denying bail.

title: Nasir Ali V. Chairman Balochistan Public Service Commission and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved a legal challenge to a public service commission's recruitment decision. Nasir Ali, who applied for the posts of District Attorney and Assistant District Attorney through the Balochistan Public Service Commission, challenged the results announced in January 2016. He argued that the recommended candidates, who had worked as Prosecuting Inspectors, did not qualify under the law because such positions did not meet the legal definition of "Pleader" or "Public Prosecutor" required for these posts. He also alleged bias by the Commission's Chairman, claiming favoritism in how marks were awarded.

The Balochistan High Court rejected these arguments. It held that Prosecuting Inspectors and Prosecuting Sub-Inspectors do perform functions equivalent to those of a Public Prosecutor under the Criminal Procedure Code, since they represent the state before magistrates and exercise similar powers and duties. Therefore, their experience qualified them to compete for the posts in question. The court also found that Nasir Ali's claims of bias against the Chairman were vague and unsupported, noting he showed no personal enmity or specific evidence of unfair treatment. The court criticized the tendency of unsuccessful candidates to make baseless accusations against recruiting authorities simply because they failed to get selected.

The petition was dismissed. The case matters because it clarifies who qualifies as a "Public Prosecutor" for prosecution service appointments and reaffirms that courts will not interfere with recruitment decisions based merely on disappointed candid

title: Fatima V. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary Ministry of Commerce, Islamabad and 2 others,
explainer:
Fatima applied for the post of Manager (Legal) at the State Life Insurance Corporation after the government ordered filling of vacant posts reserved for Balochistan under a special quota scheme. She scored the highest marks and topped the merit list. However, her appointment letter was withheld because the State Life Insurance Employees Union had filed proceedings before the National Industrial Relations Commission (NIRC) seeking to stop the recruitment process, resulting in restraining orders that delayed matters even though the union's original petition was later withdrawn.

Fatima filed a constitutional petition before the Balochistan High Court arguing that since the selection process was validly completed and she topped the merit list, the authorities could not withhold her appointment indefinitely due to a dispute that had nothing to do with her personal eligibility.

The High Court agreed with her. It held that once a merit list is finalized and made public, the department loses the power to retract the process (the principle of locus poenitentiae), and a legitimate right accrues to the top candidate. Issuing the appointment letter was merely a ministerial formality. The court applied the doctrines of legitimate expectation and promissory estoppel, ruling that the ban or restraining order could not retroactively defeat a right already earned. The court directed authorities to issue Fatima's appointment letter within one month.

This case matters because it reinforces that public authorities cannot indefinitely delay or deny appointments to candidates who have completed a fair selection process, even amid unrelated administrative or labor disputes.

title: Nasir Ali V. Chairman Balochistan Public Service Commission Koyla Phattak and 4 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a legal dispute over eligibility for prosecutorial positions in Balochistan. The petitioner, Nasir Ali, had applied for the posts of District Attorney and Assistant District Attorney through the Balochistan Public Service Commission. After taking the written examination and interview, he was disappointed to learn that other candidates, working as Prosecuting Inspectors and Prosecuting Sub-Inspectors, had been recommended for these posts instead of him. He challenged this outcome, arguing that these officials did not meet the qualification of having experience as "Public Prosecutors" or "Government Pleaders," which he claimed was required for the posts, and alleged that the Commission's Chairman acted with bias and unfairly favored certain candidates.

The core legal question was whether the roles of Prosecuting Inspector and Prosecuting Sub-Inspector count as equivalent to that of a Public Prosecutor under the Criminal Procedure Code and the Balochistan Prosecution Services Act.

The Balochistan High Court ruled against the petitioner. It held that since Prosecuting Inspectors and Sub-Inspectors perform functions before judicial magistrates similar to those of Public Prosecutors—handling duties under Sections 493, 494, and 495 of the Criminal Procedure Code—their experience should be treated as equivalent to that of a Public Prosecutor. The court reasoned that denying them eligibility despite relevant experience would violate constitutional guarantees of equality and fair treatment

title: Abdul Majeed V. Bismillah and 2 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a murder trial in Loralai, Balochistan, where one accused claimed he was a juvenile and should be tried under the Juvenile Justice System Ordinance, 2000, which provides special protections for children in criminal cases. The trial court accepted his claim of juvenility based solely on his National Database and Registration Authority (NADRA) record and a school leaving certificate, without ordering a medical examination or conducting a fuller inquiry. The complainant challenged this decision before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that the trial court acted hastily without proper investigation.

The High Court agreed with the complainant. It held that determining a person's age under the law requires a genuine inquiry, which should include a medical (ossification) test, and allowing both sides to present evidence that can be tested and challenged. NADRA records alone are not conclusive proof of age. The court noted that a claim of juvenility is a serious matter directly affecting the punishment an accused may face, so it cannot be decided casually based only on documents submitted from the bar.

As a result, the High Court set aside the trial court's order declaring the accused a juvenile and sent the matter back for a proper inquiry, including medical examination, as required by law.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that claims of juvenile status in serious criminal cases must be rigorously verified, protecting both the rights of genuine children and the integrity of the justice system against false claims of minority.

title: Shah Bakhsh V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved an appeal by Shah Bakhsh, who had been convicted by a trial court in Mastung and sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder of three people, including a minor child, under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code. The victims were found dead in a locked house that was discovered by the complainant's family.

The Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence and found serious flaws in the prosecution's case. The complainant had initially reported speaking with the accused by phone while at the deceased's house, suggesting the accused's presence there, but later omitted this detail from his court testimony. The investigating officer failed to obtain call records, collect fingerprints from blood-stained items, or send evidence for chemical analysis. No witnesses confirmed seeing the accused at the scene.

The court also examined the accused's confession and found it deeply problematic: he was given only fifteen minutes to consider it before confessing, the magistrate failed to follow proper certification procedures, did not note that an interpreter was used, and recorded conflicting dates for when the confession was taken—one date even predated the FIR itself.

Given these failures in both the circumstantial evidence and the confession's validity, the court concluded there was essentially no reliable evidence against the accused. It acquitted him, overturning the conviction and sentence.

This case highlights how procedural lapses by police and magistrates—not just weak evidence itself—can fatally undermine a criminal prosecution, entitling an accused person to acquittal on grounds of reasonable doubt.

title: Gul Mir V. The State,
explainer:
This case is from the Balochistan High Court, deciding an appeal against a murder conviction. Gul Mir was convicted by the trial court under section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code and sentenced to death for shooting his cousin's associate, Muhammad Azam, with a shotgun following an altercation. Five eyewitnesses testified to the shooting, and the incident stemmed from a fight between children of two families that escalated between the elders.

The High Court examined the evidence carefully. It found that although the motive was not initially mentioned by the complainant, this was understandable since he lived elsewhere, and other witnesses who lived nearby confirmed the background dispute. The court held that absence of proven premeditation, failure to recover the murder weapon, and minor gaps in investigation did not undermine the credibility of the eyewitness accounts, since direct ocular testimony outweighs such circumstantial shortcomings and even conflicts with medical evidence.

The court concluded that the prosecution had proven the murder charge beyond reasonable doubt, so the conviction was upheld. However, it found no evidence the killing was premeditated, and considered it possible the shooting occurred due to sudden provocation or fear during the confrontation. Because of this mitigating circumstance, the court ruled that the death penalty was too severe and reduced the sentence to life imprisonment. The appeal was dismissed, but with this sentence modification.

This case matters because it illustrates how courts distinguish between proving guilt and justifying the harshest punishment,

title: Noor Bibi and 13 others V. Meer Muhammad alias Meer Jan and 4 others,
explainer:
This case involved a family property dispute between Noor Bibi and other petitioners against Meer Muhammad and other respondents, concerning a civil suit for declaration and partition of inherited properties pending before a trial court in Lasbela.

During the trial, the petitioners wanted to present certain private witnesses who had earlier been present when the family properties were informally divided. These witnesses were sent court notices to appear, but they refused to show up. The petitioners then asked the trial court to formally summon these witnesses using its legal powers under Order XVI, Rule 10(3) of the Civil Procedure Code, which allows courts to issue arrest warrants or attach property to compel a reluctant witness to appear. The trial court rejected this request, reasoning that forcing unwilling witnesses to testify would be unfair and would only delay the case.

The Balochistan High Court disagreed and overturned the trial court's decision. It held that courts are not meant to be passive observers but must actively work to uncover the truth and resolve disputes. Since the witnesses had already been listed and served notices, the trial court had both the power and the duty to issue arrest warrants to secure their appearance rather than simply refusing to act.

The High Court ordered the trial court to issue arrest warrants for these witnesses without delay and directed that the case proceed weekly, aiming for a final decision within six months, to prevent unnecessary prolonging of the litigation.

title: Tariq Aziz V. The State,
explainer:
This is a criminal revision case from the Balochistan High Court dealing with a family tragedy and the legal rules around forgiving a murder conviction. A father and son were convicted of killing their daughter/sister after luring her mother out of the room and shooting her. Both received life imprisonment. Later, the mother (the complainant) and her son (one of the convicts) jointly asked the trial court to accept a compromise, which under Pakistani law can lead to acquittal in murder cases if properly made by the victim's legal heirs. The trial court rejected this, saying not all of the deceased's legal heirs, including other siblings, had joined the compromise.

The High Court disagreed. It explained that under Islamic law, when an unmarried person is killed, only the parents count as the "Wali" (the person with the right to forgive or compromise) unless there are none. Since the father was himself convicted of the murder, he was legally excluded from being a Wali. That left the mother as the only legal heir entitled to compromise. The other siblings were not required parties, especially since some were fugitives whose location was unknown.

The court accepted the compromise and ordered the son's release, clarifying an important point of law: a parent who commits or participates in killing their own child loses their right to be treated as an heir for purposes of compromise, leaving the surviving parent as the sole authority to forgive.

title: Janan Khan through Purchase on Installments Kaleemullah V. The State through One Battalion (Qaid) Pakistan Coastal Guard, Uthal and another,
explainer:
This case involved a vehicle seized in a narcotics smuggling operation in Balochistan. Coast Guard officials had recovered 1,052 kilograms of charas hidden in secret cavities built into a coach, leading to the arrest of the driver and conductor. Although these two men were eventually acquitted of criminal charges after trial, the Special Court (CNS) at Lasbela ordered the coach itself to be confiscated by the State.

Janan Khan, who claimed to be the real owner of the vehicle (purchased on installments), appealed this confiscation order to the Balochistan High Court. He argued he never knew about the case, had not been given notice, was not present during the trial, and had no knowledge that his vehicle was being used to smuggle drugs.

The High Court dismissed his appeal. It found his claims implausible, questioning how he remained unaware for a full year that his driver and conductor were in custody and his vehicle was impounded, especially given he supposedly relied on it for his livelihood. The documents he submitted to prove ownership were only photocopies, not properly proven through evidence or judicial inquiry.

The court did not shut the door completely, however. It advised Khan to file an application before the trial court itself, where proper evidence could be examined, and directed that court to determine whether the vehicle could be released to its owner. This case illustrates how courts require genuine evidence and timely action from those claiming property caught up in narcotics cases, rather than accepting late, unsupported claims at the appellate stage.

title: Bahawal Khan V. Rab Nawaz and another,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute in Quetta between two men claiming ownership of the same land. While a civil lawsuit over the property was pending, the complainant filed a criminal case (FIR) accusing the petitioner of forging property mutation documents. That case went to trial, and the petitioner was acquitted. Later, the same complainant filed a second FIR against the petitioner, again alleging fraud and forgery over the same property and essentially the same conduct. The petitioner asked the Balochistan High Court to quash this second FIR, arguing it violated the constitutional and legal protection against being prosecuted twice for the same offense, commonly known as double jeopardy.

The High Court examined the record, including the earlier trial and acquittal, and found that the second FIR was based on the same forged mutation and the same underlying agreement already dealt with in the first case. The court held that allowing a fresh prosecution over an issue already tried and decided amounted to double jeopardy, which is barred under Article 13 of the Constitution and Section 403 of the Criminal Procedure Code. It described the complainant's action as an abuse of the legal process and "mockery of law." As a result, the court quashed the second FIR.

This case matters because it reinforces the principle that once a person has been tried and acquitted for an offense, they cannot be dragged into another prosecution for the same facts, protecting individuals from harassment through repeated criminal complaints over settled matters.

title: Ghulam Samadani and 3 others V. Akbar khan and 3 others,
explainer:
This case is about a decades-old land dispute in Quetta. The plaintiffs claimed to be owners in possession of property that their predecessor had bought before Partition from a Hindu owner, Gordan Das. Over the years, mutations (official land records) were revised, and a rival claim emerged: the defendant argued Gordan Das had a son, Sajan Lal, who allegedly inherited and then sold part of the land to him. Both the trial court and the appellate court examined these competing claims, and the plaintiffs' suit was only partly decreed, with their appeal against the shortfall dismissed.

When the matter reached the Balochistan High Court in revision, the judge focused on a deeper problem: neither side could actually prove a valid, traceable claim to the portion of land originally belonging to Gordan Das, whose whereabouts and true heirs were never established. Since this share effectively had no verified owner, the court held it qualified as "ownerless property" under Article 172(1) of the Constitution, which deals with property that has no rightful claimant (escheat). The court ruled that neither party had established entitlement to that disputed share, and it must revert to the State. It directed the Deputy Commissioner to begin escheatment proceedings and dismissed the revision petition.

The case matters because it shows how courts handle old, unresolved property records from before Partition, especially when claimed heirs cannot be verified, ensuring such land is properly absorbed by the State rather than left in perpetual private dispute.

title: Zahid Hassan Khan V. Shams Ullah,
explainer:
This case involved a landlord, Zahid Hussain Khan, who rented out a shop for a tire business to a tenant, Shams Ullah, in 2011. When the tenant stopped paying rent after December 2012 and also failed to pay utility bills, the landlord filed for eviction under Balochistan's rent laws, citing both default in rent payment and his own need for the premises. The Rent Controller (a Civil Judge) ordered the tenant evicted but refused to order payment of the unpaid rent and utility bills, telling the landlord to pursue that separately in civil court.

The landlord appealed this partial denial to the Balochistan High Court. The High Court clarified that Rent Controllers do have the legal power under the Rent Restriction Ordinance to determine and order payment of arrears of rent and outstanding utility bills, since the law treats such bills as part of the rent obligation when the tenant is responsible for paying them. However, the court also ruled that arrears could only be awarded for up to three years before the eviction case was filed, and the landlord was not entitled to any automatically enhanced rent—any rent increase claims would need to go through separate proceedings.

This ruling matters because it clarifies the scope of a Rent Controller's authority, ensuring landlords don't have to file separate civil suits for straightforward arrears already covered by rent law, while also setting limits to prevent excessive backdated claims.

title: Abdullah and another V. Province of Balochistan through Secretary Education and another,
explainer:
This case concerned a dispute over hiring rules for Physical Education Teachers in Balochistan's schools. Under the 1984 Service Rules, as amended in 2016, candidates for this post needed both a Bachelor's degree and a Diploma in Physical Education, with at least second division marks. The petitioners held such diplomas and degrees and had applied for these teaching posts.

However, in May 2019, the Education Department issued a new Recruitment Policy that dropped the diploma requirement altogether, opening the position to a wider pool of applicants without explanation. The petitioners, who had specifically qualified themselves with the diploma, argued this change unfairly stripped away their advantage and violated their rights, since the underlying 1984 Rules had never been formally amended to remove that requirement.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the petitioners. It held that a recruitment policy, being a lower form of regulation, cannot override formally established service rules unless those rules are properly amended. Since the government had not amended the 1984 Rules or given any justification for dropping the diploma condition, the policy's silence on this point could not lawfully cancel out the rules' requirement.

The court allowed the petition and directed the authorities to reinsert the diploma requirement into the 2019 policy and to appoint teachers accordingly. The ruling reinforces the legal principle that policies and executive notifications must remain consistent with, and cannot override, statutory rules already in force.

title: A.C/SDM V. Mehrullah and another, Sui Southern Gas Company V. Mehrullah Khan and another,
explainer:
This case concerns a land dispute in Quetta, Balochistan, arising from the government's compulsory acquisition of property for the Sui Southern Gas Company's pipeline. The landowner, Mehrullah Khan, challenged both the amount of land acquired and the compensation rate set by the Assistant Commissioner (AC/SDM Saddar Quetta), who acted as the Land Acquisition Collector. He argued that only a small fraction of his land was formally awarded compensation despite more being taken, and that the rate fixed (Rs. 15 per square foot) was far below the actual market value, which he claimed was around Rs. 200 per square foot given the land's commercial and prime location.

The trial court initially dismissed his claim, but on appeal the case was sent back for fresh hearing. After a local commission inspected the site, the trial court accepted the landowner's reference and increased the compensation. The government and gas company then appealed to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the trial court's decision, finding that the Collector had improperly relied on outdated revenue records rather than considering the land's true market value, location, and commercial potential. The court also awarded 15% compulsory acquisition charges, though the landowner had waived his claim to that specific amount.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that authorities acquiring private land must fairly assess true market value, including future potential and location advantages, rather than relying on minimal official rates.

title: Muhammad Essa V. Mudasir Ahmed and others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over the registration of a second police report (FIR) arising from the same incident. After a clash between two groups, the petitioner registered an FIR against certain individuals for causing injuries and damaging his vehicle. The person he had named as an accused then went to a magistrate acting as an ex-officio Justice of Peace, seeking his own FIR to be registered giving his version of the same incident. The magistrate granted this request and ordered the police to register a separate FIR.

The petitioner challenged this before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that this violated the Supreme Court's ruling in the Sughran Bibi case, which held that when two people give conflicting accounts of the same incident, the police should not register two separate FIRs. Instead, only one FIR covers the actual offence, and any different version or counter-story should simply be recorded as part of the investigation into that same case, not treated as a fresh crime report.

The High Court agreed with the petitioner. It found that the magistrate had erred by directing registration of a new FIR instead of ordering that the other party's version be recorded within the investigation of the existing FIR. The court set aside the magistrate's order and directed investigators to record the other party's statement within the original FIR, investigate impartially, and submit a separate report to the court.

This judgment reinforces the principle that rival versions of the same incident should be investigated together, not through duplicate FIRs.

title: Sardar Khan and another V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two petitioners, Sardar Khan and another person, who faced criminal proceedings for alleged violations of the Coal Mines Regulations, 1926. After the trial court took up their case and issued summons, the petitioners repeatedly failed to appear in court. The magistrate issued non-bailable arrest warrants against them multiple times, but each time their lawyer intervened with assurances that they would appear, leading to the warrants being withdrawn without the petitioners ever actually showing up. Eventually, the petitioners filed an application under section 249-A of the Criminal Procedure Code seeking their acquittal, but this was dismissed by the trial court. They then approached the Balochistan High Court, asking it to quash the proceedings altogether as an abuse of legal process.

The High Court refused to entertain their petition. It held that a person who deliberately avoids appearing in court and evades lawful arrest is considered a fugitive from law, and such a person forfeits the right to seek the court's assistance. Relying on earlier Supreme Court and High Court rulings, the judge emphasized the principle that those seeking justice must first submit to the legal process rather than evade it. Since the petitioners had consistently dodged arrest warrants, the court ruled that allowing them to argue their case on merits would amount to rewarding non-compliance with the law. The petition was dismissed. This case reinforces the broader legal principle that courts will not assist individuals who defy judicial orders while simultaneously seeking judicial relief.

title: Muhammad Asghar and others V. The Islamic Republic of Pakistan through Secretary of Defence, Islamabad and another,
explainer:
This case involved a long-running dispute over a cinema property (Zhob Talkies) leased to a family since 1959. The petitioners' father had won a court decree in 1991 restraining the landlord from interfering with his tenancy. Decades later, when the family tried to enforce that old decree, the courts refused, saying the execution request was filed too late, beyond the time limit under Section 48 of the Civil Procedure Code. Left without a remedy, the family filed a fresh suit for a mandatory injunction to protect their tenancy rights. Both the trial court and the appellate court dismissed this new suit, reasoning that the matter was already settled and could not be relitigated (the principle of res judicata).

The Balochistan High Court disagreed with this approach. It clarified that Section 48's time limit does not apply to injunction decrees, only to other types of decrees like those involving money or property. Since the original decree combined an injunction with a declaration, and injunction decrees remain enforceable without a time limit under Order XXI Rule 32 of the CPC, the family's original decree could still be executed. The court found that the lower courts had wrongly blocked the family both from executing the old decree and from getting a fair hearing on the new suit. It set aside the earlier judgments and sent the case back for a fresh decision on merits, with evidence to be properly recorded. This matters because it protects tenants from being denied justice on technical procedural grounds when their substantive rights were never actually decided.

title: Nizam-ud-Din V. Senior Vice President and Regional Manager Operation and another ,
explainer:
This case is about a dismissed employee, Nizam ud Din, who tried to get the Balochistan High Court to review its own earlier judgment against him. Originally, his employment grievance had been dismissed by a labour court because he repeatedly failed to produce evidence despite many opportunities. His appeals to the Labour Appellate Tribunal and later to the High Court were also dismissed, mainly because they were filed too late, missing legal deadlines (limitation periods). After the High Court dismissed his constitutional petition in 2015, he filed this review application, arguing that his lawyer had mistakenly approached the wrong forum and that the delay should be excused.

The High Court rejected the review application. It explained that a review is not the same as an appeal and cannot be used to reargue or reopen a case on its merits. Review is only meant to correct clear, obvious errors in a judgment - and here, the applicant could not point to any actual mistake in the original decision. The Court also noted that the review application itself was filed about eight months late, and that every stage of the applicant's case, from his original complaint to his appeals, had suffered from delays.

The judgment reinforces an important principle: limitation laws must be applied strictly, and courts cannot indefinitely reopen settled cases simply because a party is dissatisfied with the outcome or made procedural mistakes.

title: What is Limitation in case of Declaratory Suits?

This case concerns a lawsuit filed by Abdul Majeed asking a District Judge in Zhob to officially change his recorded date of birth, based on a certificate from hospital doctors estimating his age. The suit named certain examination board and registration officials as defendants, and was decided in his favor without those parties properly contesting it. Years later, the plaintiff used this decree to get his date of birth changed in his educational degree, his national identity card, and in the record of the High Court itself, apparently to extend his service retirement date. When the High Court's Registrar noticed this irregularity, the Chief Justice took up the matter on his own initiative (suo motu) under Section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code, which allows the High Court to review lower court decisions, even without a time limit and even if no appeal was filed.

The Court also noted the plaintiff had previously given a different birth date on official forms.

The High Court set aside the original judgment and declared all resulting changes void. title: Custody of Minor on Cessation of Right of Hizanat
explainer:
This case is about who should have custody of a young boy after his parents' marriage ended in divorce.

The father and mother married in 2002, had a son in 2003, and later divorced. Custody disputes followed, and at one point the High Court had placed the child with his maternal grandmother while the parties sorted things out through the Family Court. The father then applied under the Guardian and Wards Act for custody, arguing that under Islamic law a mother's right of custody (hizanat) ends once a son reaches a certain age, and that the mother had, in any case, lost her right by remarrying. The Family Court initially granted him custody, but the appellate court reversed that decision, prompting the father to challenge it in the High Court.

The High Court dismissed the father's petition. It held that the mother's loss of hizanat rights due to remarriage does not automatically mean custody should go to the father the real and only question is the welfare of the child. The court noted that the father himself had remarried years earlier and had other children, meaning the boy would have to live with a stepmother and step-siblings, which could harm his interests. The father had also failed to pay court-ordered maintenance for years. Meanwhile, the child had been living happily and stably with his maternal grandmother for about four years. Given all this, the court ruled that the child's welfare was best served by keeping him with his grandmother, reinforcing that custody decisions must prioritize the child's actual well-being over rigid legal rules.

title: Zahoor Ahmed Mengal V. National Bank of Pakistan through President and another,
explainer:
This case involved a National Bank employee, Zahoor Ahmed Mengal, who was transferred to a new branch but was unable to report for duty due to a serious tribal enmity that threatened his life. He repeatedly wrote to the bank requesting leave, explaining his situation, but received no response. After warnings, he eventually rejoined duty, and his branch managers recommended that his absence be treated as unpaid leave rather than misconduct. Despite this, the bank issued a memorandum terminating his employment over unauthorized absence, treating the same absence period as leave without pay in one breath while firing him for it in another. He was never issued a show-cause notice, no inquiry was conducted, and he was never given a chance to defend himself before being dismissed.

The Balochistan High Court found this termination unlawful. It held that since the bank itself had already effectively condoned his absence by accepting his joining report and treating the period as unpaid leave, there was no valid ground left to terminate him. Moreover, dismissing an employee without a show-cause notice or hearing violated his basic right to fair trial and due process under the Constitution. The court set aside both the termination order and the rejection of his appeal, ordering the bank to reinstate him with full back benefits.

The judgment matters because it reinforces that employers, including banks, must follow due process, including notice and a fair hearing, before dismissing employees, and cannot punish someone for something they had already excused.

title: Bibi Zarghoona V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved two sisters, Bibi Zarghoona and another petitioner, who were accused of murdering their father. During the criminal proceedings, they reached a compromise with the deceased's legal heirs, including some minor children of the victim. Because minors cannot waive their right to compensation (Diyat) under Islamic law, the trial court ordered the sisters to pay the minors' share of Diyat in installments and granted them bail. The sisters, having no income or independent resources as women, asked the trial court to direct the State to pay this amount on their behalf, but this request was denied.

The Balochistan High Court examined existing government rules that allow the State to pay Diyat only for prisoners aged 40 or above who are stuck in jail solely due to inability to pay. Since the petitioners were younger and already released on bail, they didn't qualify. The Court found this age restriction discriminatory and against the constitutional guarantee of equality (Article 25), noting the rules unfairly created a special class based on age.

The Court ordered the trial court to investigate the sisters' actual financial situation. If they truly lacked resources, the case should be forwarded to government authorities (Home Secretary and Ministry of Human Rights) to arrange payment of the Diyat amount from Bait-ul-Mal or other funds within three months. This case matters because it highlights gaps and potential unfairness in rules meant to help poor prisoners pay compensation, and pushes for a more equitable, humane application of the law reg

title: Asadullah V. The State and another,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court in 2019, dealt with a criminal revision petition arising from a firing incident. The complainant had lodged an FIR after his brother was shot. Later, he gave a supplementary statement to police, which the trial court allowed to be formally exhibited as evidence during the trial, despite an objection from the accused's lawyer that such a statement had no legal standing beyond an ordinary statement recorded under Section 161 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The High Court ruled in favor of the accused. It held that a supplementary or further statement made by a complainant to investigators does not carry the same legal weight as the FIR itself and cannot be treated as an extension of it. Such statements can only be used for the limited purposes allowed under Section 161, not as substantive evidence to be exhibited in court. The trial court had therefore erred in allowing it to be exhibited, relying on a judgment the High Court considered incorrect.

The Court also made a broader point about trial procedure: when objections are raised during evidence recording, trial courts must decide them immediately rather than postponing the decision until the final judgment, citing a Supreme Court ruling on this point.

This decision matters because it clarifies the limited evidentiary value of supplementary statements in criminal trials and reinforces the requirement that courts resolve evidentiary objections promptly, ensuring fairer and more transparent trial procedures.

title: Abdul Ghafoor Kakar V. Honorable Balochistan High Court, through Registrar and others,
explainer:
This case involved a judicial officer, Abdul Ghafoor Kakar, who had originally served in the subordinate judiciary of Balochistan under the Balochistan High Court, but was later relieved from that service and appointed permanently as a judicial officer in Islamabad, under the Islamabad High Court, governed by the Islamabad Judicial Service Rules, 2011. He was eventually promoted to Additional District and Sessions Judge in Islamabad.

The appellant claimed he was entitled to an earlier, backdated promotion based on a 2016 Balochistan High Court judgment that granted such ante-dated promotions to certain judicial officers still serving in Balochistan. He argued that since he had originally been a permanent employee of the Balochistan judiciary, he should also benefit from that ruling.

The Balochistan High Court rejected his appeal. It held that once he was relieved from Balochistan's judiciary and appointed permanently in Islamabad, he lost any lien or claim over his former position in Balochistan. He had not been transferred or sent on deputation, and his relieving order explicitly stated he had no lien on his old post. The court also noted that promotions require performance records (PERs/ACRs) from the relevant service, which were unavailable for his time in Balochistan after 2011.

The ruling clarifies that judicial officers who move permanently between jurisdictions cannot claim retrospective benefits meant for officers still serving in their original service.

title: State through Prosecutor General Accountability, NAB V. Nisar Hussain Shah and another,
explainer:
This case involved a former government official, Nisar Hussain Shah, who served as Director General Livestock and had earlier worked as a superintendent at a sheep farm. The National Accountability Bureau (NAB) accused him of amassing extensive properties in Lahore, Quetta, Loralai and Ziarat, plus large unexplained bank deposits, all allegedly beyond what his known income could support, and of using his family members and son to hold some of these assets. The Accountability Court in Quetta tried him under the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999, but acquitted him after hearing seventeen prosecution witnesses and four defense witnesses. NAB then appealed the acquittal to the Balochistan High Court.

The High Court upheld the acquittal. It reasoned that while owning unexplained assets shifts some burden onto the accused to explain them, the prosecution still bears responsibility for proving that the explanations given were false or inconsistent with the properties. The court found that NAB's investigators had failed to properly investigate the accused's defense and had not adequately established that his claimed sources of income were illegitimate. The court also emphasized that appellate courts should be very cautious about overturning acquittals, since an acquitted person enjoys a doubled presumption of innocence. Because the investigation was flawed and the prosecution had not discharged its burden, the High Court dismissed the appeal, meaning the acquittal stood. This case highlights how weak investigation can undermine even serious corruption cases.

title: Naimatullah and 11 others V. Faizullah and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a property dispute between two families in Zhob, Balochistan. The respondents claimed a piece of land was their ancestral property based on old land records from 1952, and alleged the petitioners were trying to forcibly take possession. They sued for declaration and permanent injunction in the Qazi's Court, a special court set up under the Balochistan Civil Disputes (Shariat Application) Regulation, 1976, which applied to tribal areas. The trial court ruled in favor of the respondents, and an appellate body called the Majlis-e-Shoora upheld that decision.

The petitioners challenged this in the Balochistan High Court, arguing the appellate court's judgment was flawed because it failed to properly identify and address the key legal points in dispute, as required under procedural law, and did not give clear reasons for its decision despite receiving a detailed site inspection report.

The High Court agreed that the appellate judgment was legally defective for not following proper procedure. More importantly, it found a bigger problem: the Regulation under which these special courts operated was created using constitutional powers tied to Pakistan's tribal areas. Since the 25th Constitutional Amendment abolished that tribal status, those courts no longer had legal authority to exist. The High Court had already ordered that pending cases from such courts be transferred to ordinary civil courts. Therefore, it set aside the appellate judgment and sent the case back for fresh decision by the proper ordinary court.

title: Muhammad Ismail Muhammad Shai V. Hon'ble Chief Justice Balochistan, through Registrar and others,
explainer:
This case involved a judicial officer who claimed he was unfairly passed over for promotion in 2011 and 2014, while junior colleagues were promoted ahead of him. He argued he was never told why he was superseded and that there was nothing against him in his service record.

He first challenged this before the Balochistan Subordinate Judiciary Service Tribunal, which dismissed his appeals. He then went to the Supreme Court, which also dismissed his case but noted that if his promotion claim had merit and hadn't been properly examined, he could try filing a constitutional petition in the High Court.

He then filed these constitutional petitions before the Balochistan High Court, asking the court to grant him promotion and seniority retroactively, ahead of the colleagues who had been promoted instead of him.

The High Court dismissed the petitions. It held that administrative decisions of the Chief Justice or the High Court, such as promotion matters, are not fully shielded from constitutional review, but disputes about seniority and antedated promotion cannot be resolved through a writ petition under Article 199 of the Constitution. It also noted that the High Court had already expressed its view on the matter earlier and could not revisit it in a fresh petition.

The case matters because it clarifies the limits of constitutional court intervention in internal promotion and seniority disputes within the judiciary, reinforcing that such administrative matters are not ordinarily subject to writ jurisdiction.

title: Saira Atta V. The Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary and others,
explainer:
This case was about whether the Balochistan government could re-employ retired officers, including one particular officer, on contract or ad hoc basis against government posts. The petitioner, a qualified civil servant, argued that such re-employment was illegal because it blocked promotion opportunities for serving officers, violated Supreme Court guidelines set out in a 2013 judgment, and did not follow proper procedure or rules under the Balochistan Civil Servants Act, 1974.

By the time the case was heard, the government explained that the contract of the retired officer in question had already expired, and the post created for him had been abolished, so that specific grievance became moot.

However, the High Court still addressed the broader legal question. It held that re-employing retired civil servants must strictly follow Section 14 of the Balochistan Civil Servants Act, 1974, and related official instructions, which carry the force of law. The court emphasized that re-employment against sanctioned posts is problematic because it blocks junior officers waiting for promotion and disturbs their seniority. Such re-employment should only occur in the public interest and in exceptional cases, without blocking promotion rights. The court directed the government to avoid such appointments going forward and, where genuinely necessary, to follow the Supreme Court's guidelines carefully. The petition was disposed of with these directions, reinforcing protections for serving civil servants' promotion rights.

However, when they retired, the government paid them the Benevolent Fund based on their original, lower pay scale instead of their promoted scale. They argued this was unfair and discriminatory, since deductions were taken from the higher salary but benefits were paid based on the lower one. They filed a petition directly in the Balochistan High Court asking for the benefit to be recalculated and paid according to their promoted scale.

This means disputes about their service terms and retirement benefits must go to the Service Tribunal, not the High Court, because Article 212 specifically bars other courts from hearing such matters once a tribunal is established.

title: Messrs S.Q. Corporation through Proprietor and others V. Federation of Pakistan through Secretary Internal Affairs, Government of Pakistan, Islamabad and others,
explainer:
This case involved a business, S.Q. Corporation, that had taken finance facilities from a bank and fell into default on a large outstanding amount. The bank filed a recovery suit in court and also lodged a complaint with the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) alleging wilful default, a criminal offence under the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001. The FIA began an inquiry and issued notices to the petitioners even while the civil recovery suit was still pending before the High Court.

The petitioners argued that criminal proceedings for wilful default cannot begin until a civil court has actually determined the amount of default and fixed liability. They said the FIA's inquiry was premature and illegal, especially since an earlier, related inquiry had already been closed and was allegedly being revived through a renumbered "corrigendum."

The Balochistan High Court agreed that while the FIA does have legal power to investigate complaints of wilful default under the 2018 Rules, such a complaint can only be filed after civil liability has been properly established through the pending recovery suit. Since the bank's complaint was filed before that liability was fixed, it was premature. The court quashed the complaint and notices, but clarified the bank could file a fresh complaint once the civil suit is decided and default liability is confirmed. This ruling reinforces that criminal wilful-default proceedings must follow, not precede, civil determination of debt liability.

title: Muhammad Sajid Tareen V The Govt. of Balochistan through Chief Secretary Balochistan & others,
explainer:
This case, decided by the Balochistan High Court in 2021, dealt with the systematic exclusion of women from inheriting property during land settlement and mutation processes across the province. The petitioner brought to the court's attention that when land records were being settled, properties were often mutated only in the names of male family members, while female heirs' names were left out because revenue authorities were not making efforts to identify or include them.

The government's own response confirmed there was no proper mechanism to ensure women's inclusion before settlement. The court found that simply publishing notices in newspapers was inadequate, especially in remote areas where women often lack access to newspapers or cannot read them.

The court ruled that women's inheritance rights are protected under Islamic law and cannot be denied. It declared that any mutation or settlement excluding female heirs would be null and void, even without going to civil court. Women also could not be deprived of their share through gift deeds, relinquishments, or other pressures.

To fix this, the court ordered concrete measures: using NADRA records to verify family trees, distributing information through schools, hospitals, mosques, and loudspeaker announcements, setting up complaint cells, registering criminal cases against violators, and setting strict deadlines for deciding inheritance-related court cases. This judgment matters because it created enforceable safeguards to protect women's legal inheritance rights, which had long been ignored in practice despite existing law.

title: Saif Ud Din V. Muhi Ud Din and another,
explainer:
This case from the Balochistan High Court dealt with when police can be directed to register a criminal case (FIR) through an "ex-officio Justice of Peace" -- a role performed by a Sessions Judge under section 22-A of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The petitioner, Saif Ud Din, challenged an order by the Sessions Judge/Justice of Peace directing police to register an FIR against him based on a complaint by Muhi Ud Din. The petitioner argued that the alleged incident, supported by a medical certificate showing only minor bruises and scratches, did not amount to a cognizable offence (one serious enough for police to investigate and arrest without court permission).

The High Court agreed. It clarified that a Justice of Peace can only order registration of an FIR when the complaint discloses a cognizable offence. For non-cognizable offences, the complainant instead has two other legal routes: asking police to record the matter in the daily diary and seek a magistrate's permission to investigate, or filing a private complaint directly before a magistrate. Since no cognizable offence was made out here, the court quashed both the Justice of Peace's order and the FIR that police had registered.

Separately, the judgment also addressed police delay and confusion in complying with the court's earlier orders, with senior police officials appearing and apologizing for the lapse. The ruling is significant for clarifying the limited powers of a Justice of Peace and protecting individuals from FIRs registered without proper legal basis.

title: Taj-Ud-Din and another V. The State,
explainer:
Two men, Taj-ud-Din and Syed Muhammad, were tried for allegedly abducting a young man, Olas Khan, near Pishin and committing sodomy with him. According to the complainant, Taj-ud-Din offered him a lift, drove him away at gunpoint, and assaulted him; he was then taken back and a second assault allegedly occurred, this time involving the second accused, Syed Muhammad. The trial court convicted both men under section 364-A of the Pakistan Penal Code (kidnapping/abduction) and sentenced them to life imprisonment.

On appeal, the Balochistan High Court reviewed the evidence, including the victim's testimony, medical evidence, and recovered items such as clothing, a pistol, a mobile SIM, and cash. The court found that while the medical and circumstantial evidence supported that sodomy had occurred, the facts did not properly fit the offence of abduction under section 364-A. The court also rejected one accused's police confession as inadmissible, noting that such statements must be accepted entirely or not at all, and could not be selectively relied upon.

The High Court altered the conviction from section 364-A to section 377 (unnatural offence/sodomy) and reduced the sentence from life imprisonment to ten years for both men, while dismissing the appeal otherwise.

This case matters because it clarifies how courts must correctly match proven facts to the appropriate criminal charge, and reinforces that confessions to police cannot be used selectively as evidence.

title: Sui Southern Gas Company Ltd., Regional office and others V. Muhammad Rahim and others,
explainer:
This case involved gas theft allegations against several people accused of illegally tapping Sui Southern Gas Company (SSGC) connections in Quetta. FIRs were registered by the police against the accused under the Gas (Theft Control and Recovery) Act, 2016. However, earlier the Balochistan High Court had quashed these FIRs, holding that offences under this special law are non-cognizable, meaning police cannot register an FIR for them. Instead, the law requires that a complaint be filed directly before the special Gas Utility Court. Following the quashment, the trial court acquitted the accused persons, and SSGC challenged these acquittals through multiple appeals, which were heard together since they raised the same legal question.

The High Court upheld the earlier reasoning: because the Act contains a specific procedure (an overriding "notwithstanding" clause) requiring complaints to go before the Gas Utility Court rather than through police FIRs, registering an FIR under this Act was improper and appeared driven by ulterior motives. The court emphasized that when law prescribes a particular procedure, that procedure must be strictly followed, and citizens have a fundamental right to be treated according to law. Where authorities bypass mandated procedures, the High Court can intervene under its constitutional powers to protect citizens' rights.

This judgment matters because it reinforces that special economic offences like gas theft must follow the specific legal procedure created for them, preventing misuse of ordinary criminal process (FIRs) in matters governed by special statutes.

title: The State through Deputy Attorney General V. Zahid Khan and others,
explainer:
Four people accused of running illegal Hawala/Hundi currency exchange operations, in violation of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, 1947, were acquitted by trial courts in Quetta before their trials were even completed, using an early-acquittal provision (section 265-K, Cr.P.C.). The State, through the Federal Investigation Agency, appealed these acquittals to the Balochistan High Court.

The key issue was that FIRs against the accused were registered by FIA officials based on complaints from State Bank of Pakistan officers, but without the mandatory prior authorization from the Federal Government or the State Bank of Pakistan required under the law before such cases can be initiated. This is not a minor technicality - the law specifically requires this authorization as a safeguard before criminal proceedings can begin.

The High Court held that when a law prescribes a specific mandatory procedure, bypassing it constitutes a serious illegality that violates a citizen's fundamental rights. Since the FIA had not followed the proper legal procedure in lodging these cases, the court ruled that justice demanded the acquittals be upheld, regardless of other considerations. The court cited the principle "justice should prevail no matter if the heaven falls."

As a result, the High Court dismissed the State's appeals and upheld the acquittals in all four cases. The judgment underscores that procedural safeguards built into laws exist to protect citizens' rights, and authorities cannot ignore them even while pursuing valid investigations.

title: Hafiz Zubair and another V. Mst. Hazar Naz (Widow) and 13 others,
explainer:
This case involved a dispute over a Hajj and Umrah travel business set up as private limited companies. The original plaintiff, whose heirs later continued the case, claimed he was wrongly removed as a director and denied his 25% share and profits in one of the companies, allegedly through fake documents. He sued for a court declaration recognizing his directorship and share, cancellation of the fraudulent paperwork, and recovery of money owed to him. The trial court ruled in his favor, and an appellate court upheld that decision.

The company directors who lost then challenged the case before the Balochistan High Court, arguing that civil courts had no authority to hear the matter at all. They pointed to the Companies Ordinance, 1984, which states that only the High Court, not ordinary civil courts, can decide disputes about title or shares in a company. They argued the lower courts' judgments were void for lacking proper jurisdiction.

The High Court agreed that this was a serious problem: although the defendants had raised the jurisdiction objection early on, the trial court never formally framed it as a legal issue or decided it before proceeding to judge the rest of the case. Because determining jurisdiction first is essential, the High Court sent the case back to the trial court, directing it to specifically decide the jurisdiction question first, gathering additional evidence on that point if necessary, before proceeding further. This ensures cases are heard by the properly authorized court from the outset.

title: Ajmal and 2 others V. Additional Sessions Judge-IV, Quetta and 4 others,
explainer:
This case is about three men accused of murder and abduction who had been formally discharged from the case by the investigating officer for lack of evidence. Later, after the complainant complained about the investigation and a court ordered the case transferred to the Crimes Branch for fresh investigation, a Judicial Magistrate issued new arrest warrants for the same men and then remanded them to police custody.

The petitioners challenged this, arguing that once a charge sheet (challan) against other accused persons in the same case had already been submitted to the Trial Court (Additional Sessions Judge, Khanozai), that court alone had jurisdiction over the matter. They argued the Judicial Magistrate had no authority to issue fresh warrants or grant remand, since the case was already pending before the Trial Court.

The Balochistan High Court agreed. It held that the discharge order could only be reviewed by the Trial Court that had taken cognizance of the case after the challan was filed. The Judicial Magistrate had no jurisdiction to issue warrants or grant remand because the matter was already sub judice (pending) before the Trial Court. The Court therefore set aside the Magistrate's warrants and remand orders, and allowed the petition.

This matters because it reinforces the principle that once a case is properly before a trial court, other magistrates cannot interfere or issue conflicting orders, protecting the integrity of judicial process and jurisdictional boundaries.

title: Muhammad Saleem and others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved three men convicted by a trial court for the murder and robbery of a person, allegedly acting together to snatch money from the victim, who was then shot dead when he resisted. They appealed to the Balochistan High Court against their convictions and sentences under sections dealing with murder, robbery, and common intention.

The High Court overturned the convictions and acquitted the accused, finding the prosecution's case riddled with serious doubts. First, the sole eyewitness only gave his statement to police 24 days after the incident, with no credible explanation for the delay, making his account unreliable. Second, the witness appeared to have been introduced by the complainant rather than coming forward independently. Third, the police claimed the accused were traced through "spy information" and technology, but provided no actual evidence supporting this claim. Fourth, the identification parade meant to confirm the accused's identity was conducted improperly - inside jail premises while the accused was already under police investigation, and the witness actually failed to identify them correctly. Fifth, the weapon and bullet casing were sent for forensic testing 72 days after the crime, an unexplained delay that undermined the lab report's reliability. Finally, medical evidence wasn't properly corroborated.

The court held that these combined weaknesses meant the prosecution failed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. This case matters because it demonstrates how courts scrutinize procedural lapses - delayed statements, flawed identification parades, and forensic delays - to protect the fundamental principle that guilt must be proven conclusively

title: Ramzan and others V. The State,
explainer:
This case involved the murder of the complainant's son, who was allegedly slaughtered with a sharp weapon by several accused acting together. The First Information Report initially named unknown persons, but the complainant later named the accused in a supplementary statement. The prosecution's case largely relied on a confession one accused reportedly made before a jirga (a traditional community assembly), which was video recorded on a mobile phone by the deceased's brother and later handed over as evidence.

The Balochistan High Court found serious problems with how this evidence was handled. The video recording was never actually played in court, the accused were never given a copy or a chance to admit or challenge it, and none of the roughly 200 jirga members who witnessed the alleged confession were called as witnesses to confirm what happened. The court also noted that the investigation was mishandled twice, first by levies and then by the Crimes Branch, causing damaging delays and raising doubts about the evidence collected.

Rather than deciding guilt or innocence, the High Court sent the case back to the trial court with clear instructions: the investigating officer must prepare and provide the accused with a copy of the video, at least two jirga witnesses must be summoned, and the video must be played in court with the accused given a fair chance to cross-examine witnesses. This ruling emphasizes that confessions, even before informal community bodies, must be properly verified and tested in court before being used as evidence of guilt.

title: Muhammad Hassan V. The State,
explainer:
This case is about a man, Muhammad Hassan, who was convicted of murdering his wife by stabbing her and strangling her with a dupatta. A trial court in Dalbandin sentenced him to life imprisonment, and he appealed to the Balochistan High Court arguing there was no direct evidence against him apart from a confession recorded after his police remand period had ended, which he later retracted.

The High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the conviction. It found that Hassan himself walked into the police station the morning after the killing and voluntarily reported what he had done, even producing the blood-stained knife. The court treated this spontaneous, unprompted statement as reliable because it was made naturally, before any formal investigation began. His guilt was further confirmed by a judicial confession recorded later by a magistrate, who followed proper legal safeguards to ensure it was voluntary. The court explained that even a delayed or later-retracted confession can still support a conviction if it is shown to be true and voluntary. Additionally, medical evidence, including injuries on the body, and forensic recovery of blood-stained items matched the confession and witness accounts.

This case matters because it clarifies how Pakistani courts assess confessions and circumstantial evidence in murder cases, showing that a voluntary, corroborated confession, even if later retracted, can be sufficient to sustain a conviction.

title: Messrs Sara Enterprises Government Contractors through Proprietor V. Secretary Finance, Government of Balochistan, Quetta and 2 others,
explainer:
This case involved a government contractor who completed an irrigation construction project in 1998 under a work order from a Balochistan government department. Payment was delayed for years, leading the contractor to seek arbitration, which eventually resulted in a court decree in 2018 ordering payment. When the money was finally released in 2019, the government deducted 15 percent as tax under the Balochistan Revenue Authority Act, 2015. The contractor challenged this deduction, arguing that the tax law came into effect in 2015, long after the work was done in 1998, and therefore could not be applied to this old, completed transaction.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the contractor. It held that new laws are generally meant to apply going forward, not backward, unless the law specifically says otherwise. Since the 2015 Act did not state that it applied retrospectively, it could not be used to tax a transaction that had already been completed in 1998. The court emphasized that tax laws, which impose financial burdens, must be interpreted strictly and narrowly, and a taxpayer cannot be made liable unless they clearly fall within the law's scope.

As a result, the court declared the tax deduction illegal and void, and ordered the government to refund the deducted amount to the contractor. This case highlights the important legal principle that laws imposing taxes or liabilities cannot be applied to past events unless clearly intended by lawmakers.

title: Messrs Sara Enterprises Government Contractors through Proprietor V. Secretary Finance, Government of Balochistan, Quetta and 2 others,
explainer:
This case concerns a government contractor, Sara Enterprises, that completed an irrigation construction project for the Balochistan government in 1998 under a 1998 work order. Payment was delayed for years, leading to arbitration and eventual litigation. In 2018, a civil court decree ordered payment, and in 2019 the government finally released around Rs. 1.71 crore to the contractor. However, before payment, the Executive Engineer deducted 15 percent tax (over Rs. 25 lakh) under the Balochistan Revenue Authority Act, 2015. The contractor challenged this deduction, arguing that the 2015 law could not apply to work done back in 1998, long before the law existed.

The Balochistan High Court agreed with the contractor. It held that laws are generally presumed to apply only prospectively (to future matters), not retrospectively, unless the legislature clearly states otherwise. This is especially true for tax laws, which impose financial burdens and must be interpreted strictly and narrowly in favor of the taxpayer. Since the 2015 Act came into force well after the 1998 transaction was completed, it could not be used to tax that old, already-settled matter.

The court declared the tax deduction void and ordered the government to refund the deducted amount to the contractor. This ruling reinforces an important legal principle: new tax laws cannot be applied backward in time to reach past transactions that were already complete before the law existed, protecting citizens and businesses from unfair retrospective taxation.

title: Palwasha Sherani and others V. Pakistan Medical and Dental Council (PMDC) and others,
explainer:
This case involved medical and dental school hopefuls who failed the 2023 MDCAT (Medical and Dental College Admission Test), which is required for admission to MBBS and BDS programs. The petitioners argued the test was flawed, claiming it was conducted by an unauthorized body instead of the proper provincial authority, that the questions were too difficult and outside the syllabus, and that cheating using electronic devices had occurred during the exam. They asked the Balochistan High Court to cancel the test entirely and order a fresh one, or alternatively let them be admitted using vacant seats.

The respondents, including PMDC and the medical university, countered that the allegations were unsupported by evidence, that a committee had investigated cheating claims but found only a minor leak involving a few questions, and that thousands of students had passed the test fairly. They noted no petitioner had raised objections before taking the exam or used available complaint procedures afterward.

The court dismissed the petitions. It found the petitioners had no real evidence backing their claims, had not objected to the test's difficulty or content beforehand, and had failed to use available remedies before rushing to court. The court also noted that any seats left unfilled would simply carry forward to the next year's admissions based on province-wide merit. This ruling reinforces that courts will not interfere with academic admission processes based on unproven allegations, especially when proper procedural channels were bypassed.

title: Balochistan Bar Council through Vice-Chairman V. Government of Balochistan through Chief Secretary Balochistan, Civil Secretariat and 2 others,
explainer:
This case was about whether a government official's tenure as Member of the Balochistan Environmental Protection Tribunal could legally be extended a second time. The Balochistan Bar Council challenged a notification dated 30 December 2022 that extended the term of respondent No. 3, arguing this violated the Balochistan Environmental Protection Act, 2012 and the Balochistan Environmental Protection Tribunal Rules, 2017, which allow a member's tenure to be extended only once, for three years.

The respondent had originally been appointed Member in 2016, then given what was labeled a fresh "appointment" in 2019 (which the court treated as actually being his one permitted extension), and then extended again in 2022. The Balochistan High Court held that neither the law nor the rules permitted a second extension or any re-appointment beyond the single allowed extension. It found the 2022 extension to be an unlawful, "colourful" exercise of power by the Chief Minister, made by overlooking the relevant law, rules, and official summary. The court declared the second extension null and void from the start, set aside the notification, and ordered the government to formally remove the official from his position.

This matters because it reinforces that government appointments to statutory tribunals must strictly follow the specific rules governing tenure limits, and courts can strike down appointments made in disregard of those legal limits, even when framed as routine extensions.
